"I wasn't sure if we would be able to meet the moment, and I'm really glad that members proved me wrong, and we did," he told CNN.

His support drew attention to the race, as well as her record.

News outlets, including CNN , reported on tweets Avila Chevalier either personally wrote or reposted between 2018 and 2022 on a since-deleted account. Some — including a post that called on people to "become bad bitches" and "seize the means of production" — were written in the flippant, ironic tone favored by far-left online posters. But several made serious calls for defunding and abolishing the police and criticized Israel and Democratic politicians. After former Vice President Kamala Harris made a speech telling Central American migrants "do not come" to the United States, Avila Chevalier tweeted, "F**k Kamala Harris."

"We are the first generation to really be forming our sense of self and our political identities and our political worldviews in such a public way, and that inevitably means that we're going to say things that we'll eventually not agree with or feel cringe about or regret," she said.

Avila Chevalier said it was painful to see her deleted tweets become a distraction from the issues she wanted to highlight. It's not clear how the House Democratic Caucus will respond to Avila Chevalier or the other Justice Democrats and DSA-aligned candidates who won blue district primaries this cycle, but early indicators suggest a mix of wariness, defiance and, in some cases, cautious optimism.

Publicly, party leadership has congratulated them. But moderate Democrats are also making a point of spurning socialism to reduce the sting of Republican attacks.

Jeffries said earlier this month on NBC's Meet the Press that he rejects the national Democratic Socialists of America agenda, wants to reform but not abolish ICE and no longer supports Medicare for All after previously co-sponsoring the bill. But he acknowledged the party will have a "broad caucus" in January.

Avila Chevalier has three top priorities, what she described on the campaign trail as housing for all, "babies not bombs," and abolishing ICE. Among the 13 bills she's promised to cosponsor on her first day of Congress is Illinois Rep. Delia Ramirez's Block the Bombs Act, which would stop the unconditional transfer of offensive military weapons to Israel. She'll also back the Green New Deal, Medicare for All Act, and legislation to boost unions and raise the federal minimum wage.

Ramirez said she's been vocal with leadership about making sure Avila Chevalier as well as the other far-left primary winners feel welcome in DC. She described the New York candidate as someone who asks questions, "genuinely wants to grow, wants to learn" and wants to fight for the district.

"She also understands she can't come here and spend 20 years here before she can deliver," Ramirez said.

The likely incoming members are also still figuring out how they'll wield their influence in what could be a very narrow House Democratic majority.

"The most important thing is that we're getting into the habit of calling each other when we have questions," said Valdez, the Democratic nominee for the 7th District who is also backed by Mamdani, the DSA and Justice Democrats. "We're still figuring out what the demands will be."

In the meantime, the nominees have been focused on building up their support in their districts. For Avila Chevalier, that's meant meet-and-greets and community events.

Earlier this month she joined New York state Sen. Gustavo Rivera to hand out backpacks and school supplies to a long line of families that wrapped around a park in the South Bronx, a part of the district that heavily favored the incumbent. Rivera, who didn't endorse in the primary but said he voted for Avila Chevalier, introduced the Democratic nominee to constituents as they went through the line, often in Spanish.

"There's many people, many voters as well as electeds in this part of the district, that had a longstanding relationship with Congressmember Espaillat," Rivera told CNN in an interview at the event. "That ship has sailed. She actually won the seat. Now it's her job to actually do this type of work."

Sometimes that has forced her to confront voters whose views are far from her own. During her interview with CNN, Avila Chevalier was flagged down by a group of voters sitting in Marcus Garvey Park. The Democratic nominee struck up a conversation with Monique Wyche, a restaurant employee and small business owner who grew up in Harlem.

When Wyche brought up the Iran War, Avila Chevalier argued that the money spent on it could have gone towards universal childcare. When the topic turned to immigration, Wyche said that while ICE's actions were "sick," she was concerned about migrants not paying taxes, a claim Avila Chevalier quickly refuted.

"Actually, they do get taxed," Avila Chevalier said. "I think that narrative actually benefits corporations, and so they don't pay taxes."

The two went back and forth for nearly 10 minutes, with Wyche calling on Avila Chevalier to work with both Republicans and Democrats while also charting her own path in Congress.

That is what Avila Chevalier says she signed up for — having hard conversations with people to make sense of the world and bridge the gap between what exists and what could be – and what she hopes to bring to Congress next year.

"Organizing is about meeting people where they're at," she said. "It is deeply unsexy work."

articles.title: Jeffries responds to Kushner meeting backlash: ‘No one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass’
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Monday said “no one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass” in a post on the social media platform X. The...
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Monday said "no one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass" in a post on the social media platform X. The video comes after he faced backlash for meeting with Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law.

The New York Times reported Sunday that the two met privately ahead of November's midterms to discuss common ground on issues like housing, immigration and the high cost of living.

Jeffries said Kushner reached out to him first, and he accepted so the pair could discuss affordability. His post emphasized, however, that House Democrats have pushed the Trump administration on issues including tariffs, the Affordable Care Act, nutritional assistance and more.

"I shouldn't have to say it, but I am. No one is going to get a pass," he said. "We're going to follow the facts, apply the law, and be guided by the Constitution beginning on day one. And hold the crooks accountable."

Reactions to the meeting have been mixed. Tommy Vietor, a co-host of "Pod Save America" and former Obama aide, took to X on Sunday to criticize Kushner .

"Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals," he said.

Kushner has served as a foreign envoy for Trump, working on conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) downplayed the meeting to Fox News's Peter Doocy on "The Sunday Briefing."

"I don't know what that's about. I know Jared has interest in lots of other things going on," he said. "He's not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day to day in the White House."

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) backed Jeffries at a Monday press conference when asked whether he'd support the representative as House majority leader if Democrats take back the House in November. "I continue to support Congressman Jeffries and his bid to become the leader," Mamdani said.

Jeffries said House Democrats have "delivered results" in battling corruption. "Pam Bondi is gone. Kristi Noem is gone, and we're just getting started," he said, referring to the former attorney general and secretary of Homeland Security, respectively.

He concluded the video by discussing affordability.

articles.title: Democrat mayor blasted by DHS for 'hunting down' property owners leasing to ICE: 'Unhinged'
articles.summary: DHS calls Boston Mayor Michelle Wu's effort to dissuade property owners from leasing parking to ICE "unhinged," accusing her of hunting them down.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security is calling out Boston Democratic Mayor Michelle Wu’s "unhinged" effort to dissuade business owners from leasing to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the city, equating it to "hunting down" private property owners. After Boston banned ICE vehicles from using city-owned parking lots to stage operations, ICE issued a notice seeking to rent hundreds of parking spaces in the city for five years. In response, Wu, an outspoken opponent of President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda, issued an open letter to parking garage and lot owners throughout Boston in which she revealed the city had submitted a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request "for any local responses to ICE." DHS fired back in an X post, writing that "these actions by sanctuary Mayor Michelle Wu are unhinged." "She knows she has NO authority to block us from using private property. So, she’s hunting down private property owners and threatening them for working with ICE — because she’d rather intimidate law-abiding Bostonians than get criminal illegal aliens OFF the street," wrote DHS. TOM HOMAN FIRES BACK AT FLORIDA DEMOCRAT OVER 'RIDICULOUS' ICE RACIAL PROFILING CLAIM ICE issued a "sources sought" notice last month for "surge parking" in 14 cities across the country. The notice revealed ICE was seeking 249 contiguous parking spaces in Boston. In response, Wu issued an official appeal from the city of Boston for garage and lot owners to "reject ICE staging facilities." She wrote that "were ICE to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region." She boasted that she "joined together with six other cities across Greater Boston and signed Executive Orders prohibiting ICE from staging its operations on municipal property and parking lots," adding, "Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston." Wu also noted that the same day, the city submitted a FOIA request for any local responses to ICE. She told the garage and lot owners, "We will keep you updated as we push for a response," adding, "Thank you again for your partnership." EXCLUSIVE: 5-TIME ILLEGAL ENTRANT ADMITS ‘MISTAKE’ THAT FINALLY GOT HIM BUSTED BY ICE In its FOIA request, which was submitted to ICE and reviewed by Fox News Digital, the city of Boston states that it is seeking "all submissions and/or responses to ICE Sources Sought Notice with Notice ID ‘DHS-ICE-SurgeParking.’" DHS responded to Wu’s FOIA request by calling her a "pro-criminal illegal alien politician" in another X post. The agency said the request also indicates that Wu "admits she has no authority to block ICE from utilizing private property." "If private citizens want to allow federal law enforcement onto their own property, they should be allowed to do so—free of threats, intimidation and coercion from their radical left-wing mayor who shamelessly compared ICE agents to a neo-Nazi group," wrote DHS. Fox News Digital reached out to Wu’s office and the city of Boston for comment. Wu’s FOIA request came after the Boston City Council adopted an "emergency resolution" earlier this month urging the city to "explore all avenues to oppose" proposed parking leases for ICE in downtown Boston. TOM HOMAN EXPLAINS IMMIGRATION STRATEGY FOCUSING ON SANCTUARY CITIES SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The council said that by adopting the emergency resolution, it was calling on the city to "explore available options to prevent the proposed parking leases and expressed its opposition to an increased ICE presence in the city." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Besides Boston, ICE’s notice showed the agency seeking significant numbers of parking spaces in the metropolitan areas of Denver, Seattle, Philadelphia, Dallas, Phoenix, Pittsburgh and several other cities.

articles.title: Florida, hard-hit by Obamacare drop-off, feels the squeeze of rising healthcare costs
articles.summary: Florida chef Elijah Button was chopping onions in June when his knife slipped and sliced his middle finger to the bone.  After Republicans in Congress let en...
articles.body:
ST. CLOUD, Fla. (AP) — Florida chef Elijah Button was chopping onions in June when his knife slipped and sliced his middle finger to the bone.

It was his worst kitchen accident to date. But having given up his Affordable Care Act health insurance plan in January because of a $100 monthly premium hike he couldn't afford, the 21-year-old in St. Cloud didn't have the money for emergency care.

"Going to the hospital for it wasn't even an option," he said, gesturing toward his finger before preparing a pot roast for his aunt and uncle in their suburban home. "My first thought was, 'how am I going to fix this?'"

After Republicans in Congress let enhanced federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans expire in January, millions of Americans including Button had to decide whether to keep insurance that often doubled or tripled in cost — or risk going without it.

Months later, with no action from lawmakers to replace the lost funds, they're facing the consequences. Some are dealing with strained budgets and exorbitant medical bills, while others avoid the doctor in fear of the cost.

Florida, whose large population of gig workers, entrepreneurs and small business owners relies heavily on the federal health insurance marketplace, has become one of the nation's most visible epicenters of that impact.

Figures first reported by The Associated Press showed that about 440,000 Floridians dropped their Affordable Care Act plans this year — more than in any other state . Thousands more who kept coverage are struggling to get by, as prices of necessities like groceries and gasoline remain steep, and health insurers project another year of double-digit premium hikes .

While Florida had the most affected residents, its struggles are reflective of broader nationwide concerns over rising healthcare costs and a lack of meaningful policy to address them.

In the deep-red state where congressional districts were recently redrawn to strongly favor Republicans, the cost of healthcare is a major campaign issue. Republican midterm candidates have been promoting fraud crackdowns to protect federal health programs, while Democrats have been urging voters to help Congress change hands so they can restore subsidies.

Button, who is estranged from his parents, asked his uncle for help with his bloodied finger. With a butterfly bandage, splint and daily cleanings and dressings, it healed. But the scar still gnaws at Button as a symbol of what else could go wrong.

"It just feels like I'm living in a house of cards," he said.

Florida's population and politics make it ground zero for ACA fallout

Last fall, debate over the expiring subsidies consumed Congress, resulting in a record 43-day government shutdown as Democrats insisted on extending the COVID-era assistance and most Republicans refused.

Fast forward almost a year and lawmakers rarely reference the topic anymore. The administration says it is addressing affordability with fraud-busting efforts and deals with drug companies, but Congress hasn't passed any significant legislation to lower health costs.

In part due to its large number of construction, hospitality and small business workers — and also because its Republican-led legislature never expanded the Medicaid safety-net health program — Florida has the largest Affordable Care Act enrollment in the country. At just over 3.8 million enrollees, it represents about a fifth of the nation's total enrolled population.

Of the roughly 443,000 Floridians who left the marketplace, most are likely going without insurance, according to Cynthia Cox, a vice president at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF. She said that's because it is typically a "place of last resort" to get coverage.

The data doesn't tell the stories of those who kept insurance. Tracy Rand, a licensed mental health counselor in Leesburg, Florida, is one of them.

Ever since getting her ovaries removed last year due to benign but painful tumors, she has had severe menopause symptoms that require medication, including an overactive bladder and hot flashes that cause piercing headaches.

She uses clear plastic containers to organize the more than 30 medicines and supplements she takes daily, their bottles crammed into a living-room drawer and a tray on her kitchen counter.

The 51-year-old's Affordable Care Act plan was going to surge in price this year from $55 a month to $1,100 a month, so she downgraded. Her new plan, with higher deductibles and copays, costs $160 a month.

To make that work in her budget, Rand quit a doctoral program she was working toward, started buying groceries at cheaper stores, gave up once-monthly dinners out with her husband and stopped meeting friends regularly at a paint-your-own pottery studio.

It's been a difficult adjustment, but a necessary one for her health.

Rand said the prospect of insurers raising rates again fills her with dread.

"I don't know what else we can get rid of," she said, covering her face with her hands. "I don't know if we're going to have to file bankruptcy.″

Clinics for the uninsured are a saving grace — but they can't take everyone

In Orlando's leafy, brick-paved neighborhood of Colonialtown South, Tarsha Watson found her lifeline. A clinic there called Grace Medical Home provides low-income, uninsured Floridians with comprehensive care for a $5 per-visit fee.

Watson, 54, has a master's degree in business administration, but she hasn't been able to find work since losing her job two years ago. That means she doesn't have health insurance. When she explored Affordable Care Act coverage, she was quoted $600 per month, far out of her reach.

At Grace, Watson learned her blood sugar is high and that she needed to lose weight. Now, she walks laps around her backyard pool and does Tai Chi YouTube tutorials to focus on fitness. She said she wishes everyone could have her experience.

"It's very hard out here," she said. "It's not enough."

At the clinic, patients cycle in and out of a wide hallway lined with appointment rooms as doctors scan supply shelves for complimentary over-the-counter medications. The expansive building has separate areas for dental, mental health, vision and pediatric care.

CEO Stephanie Garris said it's one of 110 free or charitable clinics in Florida, but that's not enough to handle demand. To treat more people in response to the Affordable Care Act changes, it recently started hosting a mobile acute care clinic for walk-in patients.

Garris said Grace Medical Home treated about 1,350 people last year. Every year, they take about 350 new patients.

"Would I love to double that, triple that? Of course," Garris said. "I just think in the reality, with the huge number of uninsured that we have, it's just not possible."

Health costs become an issue in midterm campaigns

For U.S. Rep. Darren Soto, a Democrat defending his seat in a sprawling — and now much redder — redrawn district south of Orlando, health costs are a campaign focal point.

He said his district, which is near various theme parks, had the second-largest Affordable Care Act enrollment in the nation, in part because many small tourism businesses can't offer employees health insurance.

"I just hear it everywhere I go," he said. His Republican opponent, Navy veteran and former Trump administration official Dan Green, did not answer emailed questions about the subsidies but has emphasized affordability of groceries and property insurance as campaign priorities.

Soto voted with Democrats and some Republicans — including a few from Florida — to save the subsidies last year. The Republican majority declined and suggested other ideas, including funding Americans' health savings accounts. No law along those lines has passed yet.

Button, a Democrat in Soto's district, said he is open to different reforms for health costs, but said politicians aren't acting fast enough.

"They keep trying to make excuse after excuse," he said. "I don't have six months to a year to wait for you guys to pass this through the hoops that you need to."

articles.title: Trump says US considering renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Trump's remarks come amid a deepening cross-border trade feud that has increasingly centered on Ontario Premier Doug Ford.
articles.body:
Minister of Industry of Canada, Mélanie Joly, has responded to President Donald Trump's comments that the United States is giving "serious consideration" to renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," Joly told reporters on Tuesday when asked about Trump's statement, the latest escalation in his increasingly bitter dispute with Canada as trade talks between the two countries remain stalled. "We're proud of the Great Lakes… and we'll stand up for what we have," she said. "I really think that, with all these shenanigans happening. We'll just be smart and we'll be strategic, and we'll fight back."

In a Tuesday post on Truth Social, Trump had suggested the move was under consideration because the U.S. did not expect to be "doing much business with Ontario any longer." The president later shared on his social-media platform a map of the lake with its current name crossed out and replaced with "Lake America." The proposal lands as relations between Washington and Ottawa are under fresh strain following the breakdown of trade talks and months of sparring between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

"It is quite possible that Canadians could see the appropriation of Lake Ontario and its renaming as part of the larger effort on the part of the U.S. to exert its influence territorially," Derek Alderman, a cultural and historical geographer, told Newsweek . He added that the move seemed intended "to exert some advantage or strength in the trade war with Canada."

Meanwhile, Reuben Rose-Redwood, Professor of Geography at the University of Victoria, called it "pure rage bait" and a "well-worn move from the Trump playbook akin to calling Canada the '51st State' or renaming the Gulf of Mexico to capture media attention."

"Trump's threat to rename Lake Ontario is pure rage bait aimed at stoking anger among Canadians while distracting Americans from the fact that Trump overplayed his hand in the trade negotiations with Canada," he told Newsweek .

The official White House X account later shared a map of the United States, in the style of Lego, which labelled the lake which borders New York as "Lake America."

However, it appears that the map is incorrect with D.C. labeled as being located in North Carolina in the White House's map.

"How much drinking water did you idiots use up just to put DC and NJ in the wrong places?" The Lincoln Project asked in response to the post on X, referring to the assumption that the map was created via AI.

Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly says "we'll always call it Lake Ontario" in response to Trump's threat to rename it "Lake America" pic.twitter.com/Md9OH9hwNr — CSPAN (@cspan) August 25, 2026

Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly says "we'll always call it Lake Ontario" in response to Trump's threat to rename it "Lake America" pic.twitter.com/Md9OH9hwNr

Newsweek has contacted Ford's office and the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for comment.

The White House referred Newsweek to Trump's Truth Social post when approached for clarification on his proposal.

The president's remarks come following the breakdown of trade talks between U.S. and Canadian negotiators on Friday.

Carney said last-minute changes by the American side were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," while U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer blamed Canada for the breakdown and told CNBC's Squawk Box that Ottawa's negotiators sought their own 11th-hour additions.

The U.S. has now imposed 50 percent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian products —targeting certain motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages, and dairy, as well as a host of other goods together worth around $20 billion—and Trump has threatened the same duties on Canadian cars, automotive parts and steel.

Prime Minister Carney has said the country will match these "dollar for dollar," and Ottawa is preparing to announce a specific set of countermeasures as soon as Tuesday which will come into effect in September.

Ford has emerged as one of the most vocal opponents of the administration's Canada policies. Ford has previously threatened trade retaliation and restriction s affecting exports to the U.S., making Ontario a frequent focus of Trump's criticism as tensions between the neighboring countries intensify.

Ford has said that his country was prepared for "an economic war." He told the Associated Press that "everything was on the table" when it came to responding to the new tariffs, including limiting restricting electricity exports and critical mineral supplies from Ontario.

Ford made a similar threat early last year, shortly after Trump's return to office and following the announcement of tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.

The cross-border trade feud between the historic allies has often centered on Ford, who on Monday called Trump a dictator and said during a news conference in Hamilton that the U.S. president could "kiss my a**."

📍 Lake America pic.twitter.com/zqDh8pXkoq — The White House (@WhiteHouse) August 25, 2026

📍 Lake America pic.twitter.com/zqDh8pXkoq

— The White House (@WhiteHouse) August 25, 2026

Lake Ontario is one of North America's five Great Lakes, sitting on the U.S.-Canada border between Ontario and New York. It is the smallest Great Lake by surface area but serves as a key shipping link between the Great Lakes region and the Atlantic Ocean through the St. Lawrence Seaway. Major cities on its shores include Toronto, Hamilton and Rochester.

The city derives its name from the lake, which got it from an indigenous word predating both Canada and the United States. It is usually traced to the Wyandot (Huron) word Ontarí'io or a related Iroquoian term, variously translated as "great" or "beautiful" water.

Rose-Redwood said that while the Trump administration can order the name to be changed on U.S. federal maps, it has no power over whether Canada or international map makers do so. The last time Trump announced he was altering the name of a location, the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, other countries failed to follow suit.

"Trump can certainly instruct the U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to rename Lake Ontario on U.S. federal maps, yet Canadian and international mapmakers are not obliged to comply with any decrees coming from the White House," Rose-Redwood told Newsweek .

"Although President Trump's threat of a name change is meant to exert some advantage or strength in the trade war with Canada that has ensued, it actually could backfire by further alienating the Canadian people," said Alderman, a former president of the American Association of Geographers. "Place names are quite important to people's identity as well as key resources in educating our youth and being key parts of treaties, policy documents and maps used for a variety of economic and political activities."

Alderman, now a professor in the University of Tennessee's Geography & Sustainability Department, told Newsweek that such a change would only exacerbate fears that Trump is hoping to turn the country into a "51st state," while also threatening Canadian identity.

"On a deeper level, the president's abrupt and unilateral threat to rename Lake Ontario, seemingly without proper public discussion or governmental deliberation, would say something negative about how the names on our maps, landscapes and bodies of water are being reduced to pawns and weapons in the latest battles over trade negotiation and insults traded between U.S. and Canadian leaders," he added.

The proposal would also create an unexpected classroom headache. Generations of students have memorized the Great Lakes using the acronym "HOMES" for Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior. A different name for Lake Ontario would render the mnemonic obsolete.

The name Lake Ontario predates both the United States and Canada and has Indigenous origins.

The name is generally traced to an Iroquoian term, often rendered as Ontarí'io or Ontario , which has been interpreted as meaning "great lake" or "beautiful water." The precise linguistic origin and meaning have been debated, but the name was in use long before European settlement and eventually became the name used for the lake and the province of Ontario.

That history gives the proposed name change an additional cultural dimension. Lake Ontario is not simply a label on a modern map: its name is connected to Indigenous languages and centuries of history in the Great Lakes region.

The lake's name was subsequently adopted by the province of Ontario, which was established as a British North American province in 1867 and later became Canada's most populous province.

A move by the U.S. to refer to the lake as "Lake America" on federal maps would therefore place a modern political label over a name with a much longer history.

Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area, but it is considerably deeper than its size might suggest.

The president has also shown a willingness to use provocative place-naming proposals as a political statement. Earlier this month, he shared an image on Truth Social depicting the Strait of Hormuz as "NEW U.S. Territory" and publicly entertained the idea of asserting U.S. control over the strategically important waterway.

paragraphs: Minister of Industry of Canada, Mélanie Joly, has responded to President Donald Trump's comments that the United States is giving "serious consideration" to renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," Joly told reporters on Tuesday when asked about Trump's statement, the latest escalation in his increasingly bitter dispute with Canada as trade talks between the two countries remain stalled. "We're proud of the Great Lakes… and we'll stand up for what we have," she said. "I really think that, with all these shenanigans happening. We'll just be smart and we'll be strategic, and we'll fight back."

In a Tuesday post on Truth Social, Trump had suggested the move was under consideration because the U.S. did not expect to be "doing much business with Ontario any longer." The president later shared on his social-media platform a map of the lake with its current name crossed out and replaced with "Lake America." The proposal lands as relations between Washington and Ottawa are under fresh strain following the breakdown of trade talks and months of sparring between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

"It is quite possible that Canadians could see the appropriation of Lake Ontario and its renaming as part of the larger effort on the part of the U.S. to exert its influence territorially," Derek Alderman, a cultural and historical geographer, told Newsweek . He added that the move seemed intended "to exert some advantage or strength in the trade war with Canada."

Meanwhile, Reuben Rose-Redwood, Professor of Geography at the University of Victoria, called it "pure rage bait" and a "well-worn move from the Trump playbook akin to calling Canada the '51st State' or renaming the Gulf of Mexico to capture media attention."

"Trump's threat to rename Lake Ontario is pure rage bait aimed at stoking anger among Canadians while distracting Americans from the fact that Trump overplayed his hand in the trade negotiations with Canada," he told Newsweek .
The official White House X account later shared a map of the United States, in the style of Lego, which labelled the lake which borders New York as "Lake America."
However, it appears that the map is incorrect with D.C. labeled as being located in North Carolina in the White House's map.

"How much drinking water did you idiots use up just to put DC and NJ in the wrong places?" The Lincoln Project asked in response to the post on X, referring to the assumption that the map was created via AI.

Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly says "we'll always call it Lake Ontario" in response to Trump's threat to rename it "Lake America" pic.twitter.com/Md9OH9hwNr — CSPAN (@cspan) August 25, 2026
Minister of Industry of Canada Mélanie Joly says "we'll always call it Lake Ontario" in response to Trump's threat to rename it "Lake America" pic.twitter.com/Md9OH9hwNr
Newsweek has contacted Ford's office and the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for comment.
The White House referred Newsweek to Trump's Truth Social post when approached for clarification on his proposal.
The president's remarks come following the breakdown of trade talks between U.S. and Canadian negotiators on Friday.

Carney said last-minute changes by the American side were "unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," while U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer blamed Canada for the breakdown and told CNBC's Squawk Box that Ottawa's negotiators sought their own 11th-hour additions.

The U.S. has now imposed 50 percent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian products —targeting certain motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages, and dairy, as well as a host of other goods together worth around $20 billion—and Trump has threatened the same duties on Canadian cars, automotive parts and steel.

Prime Minister Carney has said the country will match these "dollar for dollar," and Ottawa is preparing to announce a specific set of countermeasures as soon as Tuesday which will come into effect in September.

Ford has emerged as one of the most vocal opponents of the administration's Canada policies. Ford has previously threatened trade retaliation and restriction s affecting exports to the U.S., making Ontario a frequent focus of Trump's criticism as tensions between the neighboring countries intensify.

Ford has said that his country was prepared for "an economic war." He told the Associated Press that "everything was on the table" when it came to responding to the new tariffs, including limiting restricting electricity exports and critical mineral supplies from Ontario.
Ford made a similar threat early last year, shortly after Trump's return to office and following the announcement of tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.

The cross-border trade feud between the historic allies has often centered on Ford, who on Monday called Trump a dictator and said during a news conference in Hamilton that the U.S. president could "kiss my a**."

articles.title: Opinion - A MAGA plot to keep power in Congress if they lose the election?
articles.summary: He will scare them away from the polls by posting federal agents at their voting places or discouraging them by disparaging mail-in ballots.
articles.body:
Democrats are widely expected to win control of the House in November's election. The Senate remains a tossup. But there is a nagging suspicion that Trump will somehow pervert the will of the people to ensure that Republicans retain their majority in the House and somehow steal the election.

Here's his playbook: For starters, MAGAs will demonize the Democrats. Evoking Senator Joseph McCarthy, President Trump has already referred to Democrats as "hard core, godless Communists."

Republican House majority leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) said , "The Bolshevik takeover of the Democratic Party is in full swing, and communism is on the ballot this November."

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) posted , "The question before Congress is whether we will preserve our constitutional republic OR chart a fundamentally different course that leads us down the ROAD TO COMMUNISM."

Trump will delegitimize eligible voters. He will scare them away from the polls by posting federal agents at their voting places or discouraging them by disparaging mail-in ballots.

But here's the crusher: If the outcome is close, his minions can refuse to seat elected Democrats by reason of a yawning loophole in how congressional elections are administered. But beware! If Republicans try this one on the Democrats, and the Democrats at some point reverse positions, you can count on them to return the compliment next election. The bottom-line of such an action will be constitutional chaos.

The Constitution provides : "Each house shall be the judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members." Those decisions are not reviewable by the courts . This leaves an opportunity for presumptive Speaker-in-waiting Johnson to deny Democratic members-elect their seats in the 120th Congress.

A losing House candidate may contest his or her election. The issue is decided by a simple majority vote. The new House can refuse to seat the winner while the challenge is pending. If things are close, Republicans may even temporarily hold a majority. Thus, even if Democrats only narrowly win a House majority, one or more defeated Republican candidates might try to deny office to their Democratic opponents. The Senate has its own rules for dealing with contested elections and normally seats the certified winner without prejudice.

We are accustomed to voters having final say, but this has not always been the case. Jeffrey Jenkins , a Professor of Law at USC Price determined there have been 601 election contests in the House between 1789 and 2002 — an average of around 5.6 per Congress.

In 2021 Mike Pence followed the advice of his courageous lawyer, retired Judge J. Michael Luttig, who persuaded him that our constitutional traditions required an orderly transfer of power and the election result must be respected. The same quandary may be unfolding now. And Johnson is no Mike Pence. A card-carrying election-denier, Johnson once filed a brief in the Supreme Court claiming there were "unconstitutional irregularities" in 2020 election outcomes.

That is exactly why I fear that Republicans have a legal loophole to subvert the will of the people. The 2026 midterms could thus be a decisive test of U.S. democratic norms, with the potential for a constitutional crisis if elected members are denied seats.

As the 2020 election conspiracies illustrate, the challenges could be based on virtually anything. Defeated contestants could claim that their state's refusal to turn over voter rolls to the Trump administration meant the election was corrupt. They could argue that the Senate's refusal to pass the SAVE Act allowed illegal immigrants to vote for their opponents in large numbers. They could try to cast doubt on mail-in ballots.

The brooding omnipresence in the midterms is Trump, whose endorsements have already proved to be the kiss of death. One thing is clear about Trump — most Americans don't like him. His job approval rating stands at 33 percent in a new Reuters-Ipsos poll of adults , with 63 percent disapproving.

Trump has a big stake in the outcome aside from just his hatred of losing. He does not want to face congressional investigations, much less potential impeachment for corruption.

So, what's the answer? Only an unambiguous election landslide will scotch Trump and his movement. That's what dethroned Viktor Orban in Hungary. But there is no prospect that such a landslide is imminent. The influential Cook Political Report lists 18 tossup races in the House out of 435. A further 19 races lean Democratic or Republican. Even taken together, it means less than 10 percent of House races that will prove decisive.

So, it is entirely possible that we will run a reprise of 2020, when the outcome of a narrow election beclouded with accusations of fraud, and MAGA determined to retain control. The hope is only fleeting that men like Johnson have enough honesty and integrity to keep the nation from a constitutional crisis.

Whatever you learned in school, it is ultimately the House and the Senate deciding who sits in Congress — not the American people.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: Jackson rips into Supreme Court colleagues' 'serious legal error' on Trump mail-in voting order
articles.summary: Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson warns of election chaos in a 23-page dissent as the Supreme Court lets Trump's mail-voting executive order proceed.
articles.body: Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson sharply rebuked her colleagues' decision allowing the Trump administration to move forward with parts of its mail-voting executive order, warning that the ruling could create election chaos and leave states trapped between filing legal challenges too early or too late. "This ruling violates well-established precedents concerning this Court’s equitable discretion and needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections," the Court's junior liberal justice wrote in a 23-page dissent Monday. Jackson said the decision "lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges." The court granted the Trump administration’s request to stay a lower-court injunction that had blocked implementation of portions of President Donald Trump’s March executive order in 23 Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia. TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS The unsigned majority opinion did not decide whether the executive order itself is lawful. Instead, the court concluded that the administration was likely to prevail on its argument that the states’ challenge was premature because they had not yet suffered a sufficiently concrete injury. "The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful," the majority wrote. "On that score, time will tell." Jackson took aim at that reasoning, arguing that the states were already confronting election-planning costs, threats of prosecution and uncertainty over possible changes to mail-ballot procedures. JACKSON PUBLICLY AIRS GRIEVANCES WITH CONSERVATIVE COLLEAGUES OVER TRUMP-ERA RULINGS She accused the majority of embracing what she called a "Catch-Me-If-You-Can approach" that could make it difficult for states to determine when an election-related challenge is ripe for judicial review. The court has previously warned against courts changing election rules too close to Election Day. Jackson argued Monday’s decision creates the opposite problem by telling states that some challenges can also come too early. "The Court does a disservice to all concerned by distorting Article III standing and ripeness principles to issue a ruling that contributes to pre-election chaos instead of quashing it," she wrote. Jackson also accused the majority of a "lack of situational awareness," arguing that the administration was seeking emergency relief while simultaneously maintaining that the consequences of the executive order remained uncertain. Trump’s March 31 executive order directs the Department of Homeland Security to take steps toward compiling state-specific lists of U.S. citizens and instructs the attorney general to prioritize certain investigations and prosecutions involving allegedly ineligible voters. The order also directs the U.S. Postal Service to pursue rules governing mail-in and absentee ballots, including ballot-envelope requirements, tracking barcodes and state-specific voter lists. FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS POSTAL SERVICE FROM CARRYING OUT TRUMP MAIL-IN BALLOT ORDER The Postal Service outlined plans last week for implementing portions of the order, according to The Associated Press, though the approaching election calendar could limit how much can take effect before November. North Carolina is scheduled to begin sending ballots to military and overseas voters Sept. 4, with other states following soon afterward. Justice Sonia Sotomayor filed a separate dissent joined by Justice Elena Kagan, arguing that the states already faced sufficiently concrete and imminent injuries to bring their challenge. The litigation will continue in the lower courts. The Supreme Court’s order stays the Massachusetts injunction while the administration’s appeal proceeds in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit and potentially returns to the Supreme Court. Jackson closed her dissent by calling the case "not a close call," and arguing that allowing the administration to proceed risked confusion and last-minute disruption ahead of the midterms. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "When the Government’s obvious goal is to interfere with the Plaintiff States’ practices and prerogatives in a manner that the Constitution does not authorize," Jackson wrote, "it is both a serious legal error and a grave misuse of our equitable emergency powers to let the Executive proceed even one step further." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: US judge blocks Ohio law requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration
articles.summary: By Luc Cohen Aug 25 (Reuters) - A U.S. judge on Tuesday blocked an Ohio law requiring residents to present documentary proof of citizenship when registering...
articles.body:
Aug 25 (Reuters) - A U.S. judge on Tuesday blocked an Ohio law requiring residents to present documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote at the battleground state's motor vehicles offices, in the latest ‌setback for allies of President Donald Trump pushing to tighten voter registration rules.

The decision by Cleveland-based U.S. District Judge ‌Solomon Oliver Jr. marked a defeat for Ohio's Republican government ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. A competitive race for a Senate seat in the ​state is considered critical for Democrats' hopes of winning control of the Senate.

Trump and fellow Republicans in state governments across the country are pushing more restrictions on voter registration, based in part on claims of widespread voting by non-U.S. citizens. Democrats and voting rights advocates counter that non-U.S. citizen voting is rare and that greater restrictions can make it harder for U.S. citizens to vote.

In Ohio, Governor Mike ‌DeWine last year signed a new law requiring ⁠people to present documents such as a birth certificate, a passport or a naturalization certificate when registering to vote while applying for a driver's license or another type of state identification document.

Advocacy groups including the Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans sued to challenge the law, arguing that it imposed an unnecessary obstacle to registering to vote in violation of the National Voter Registration Act, a 1993 federal law that sought to expand voter registration in part by ​requiring states ​to give people the opportunity to register to vote when they ​apply for driver's licenses.

In issuing a preliminary injunction on ‌Tuesday siding with the advocacy groups, Oliver wrote that having voters attest in writing that they are U.S. citizens was enough to allow Ohio election officials to assess their eligibility to vote.

The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, wrote that NVRA had succeeded in expanding voter registration.

Ben Stafford, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said in a statement, "Eligible Ohioans will now have the opportunity to register to vote at the BMV without having to produce unnecessary paperwork."

Stafford's firm, Elias Law Group, frequently represents the Democratic Party in ‌court.

The office of Ohio's attorney general, which is representing ​the state in court, did not immediately respond to a request for ​comment.

After the lawsuit was filed, Secretary of State Frank LaRose, ​Ohio's top election official, said in a statement, "It's common sense that only U.S. citizens should be on ‌our voter rolls. I won't apologize for, or back ​down from the work we ​do to ensure the integrity of our voter rolls."

Trump has unsuccessfully pushed Congress to pass a nationwide law, known as the SAVE Act, that would require Americans to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote, arguing it would ​deliver Republicans a "guaranteed" win in November.

A Reuters investigation ‌in July undercut Trump's portrayal of non-U.S. citizen voting as part of a broad Democratic Party conspiracy, finding ​that federal prosecutors have charged just 129 people under a federal "voting by aliens" statute created by Congress in ​1996.

(Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by Alistair Bell)
paragraphs: Aug 25 (Reuters) - A U.S. judge on Tuesday blocked an Ohio law requiring residents to present documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote at the battleground state's motor vehicles offices, in the latest ‌setback for allies of President Donald Trump pushing to tighten voter registration rules.

The decision by Cleveland-based U.S. District Judge ‌Solomon Oliver Jr. marked a defeat for Ohio's Republican government ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. A competitive race for a Senate seat in the ​state is considered critical for Democrats' hopes of winning control of the Senate.

Trump and fellow Republicans in state governments across the country are pushing more restrictions on voter registration, based in part on claims of widespread voting by non-U.S. citizens. Democrats and voting rights advocates counter that non-U.S. citizen voting is rare and that greater restrictions can make it harder for U.S. citizens to vote.

In Ohio, Governor Mike ‌DeWine last year signed a new law requiring ⁠people to present documents such as a birth certificate, a passport or a naturalization certificate when registering to vote while applying for a driver's license or another type of state identification document.

Advocacy groups including the Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans sued to challenge the law, arguing that it imposed an unnecessary obstacle to registering to vote in violation of the National Voter Registration Act, a 1993 federal law that sought to expand voter registration in part by ​requiring states ​to give people the opportunity to register to vote when they ​apply for driver's licenses.

In issuing a preliminary injunction on ‌Tuesday siding with the advocacy groups, Oliver wrote that having voters attest in writing that they are U.S. citizens was enough to allow Ohio election officials to assess their eligibility to vote.
The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, wrote that NVRA had succeeded in expanding voter registration.
Ben Stafford, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said in a statement, "Eligible Ohioans will now have the opportunity to register to vote at the BMV without having to produce unnecessary paperwork."
Stafford's firm, Elias Law Group, frequently represents the Democratic Party in ‌court.
The office of Ohio's attorney general, which is representing ​the state in court, did not immediately respond to a request for ​comment.

After the lawsuit was filed, Secretary of State Frank LaRose, ​Ohio's top election official, said in a statement, "It's common sense that only U.S. citizens should be on ‌our voter rolls. I won't apologize for, or back ​down from the work we ​do to ensure the integrity of our voter rolls."

Trump has unsuccessfully pushed Congress to pass a nationwide law, known as the SAVE Act, that would require Americans to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote, arguing it would ​deliver Republicans a "guaranteed" win in November.

A Reuters investigation ‌in July undercut Trump's portrayal of non-U.S. citizen voting as part of a broad Democratic Party conspiracy, finding ​that federal prosecutors have charged just 129 people under a federal "voting by aliens" statute created by Congress in ​1996.
(Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by Alistair Bell)

articles.title: ICE arrests jumped to nearly 50,000 in July, the highest monthly total of Trump’s second term
articles.summary: The spike in immigration arrests shows that the administration has continued to advance its mass deportations agenda despite a shift in approach earlier this...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested nearly 50,000 people in July , the highest single monthly arrest total during the second Trump administration, according to new figures.

The spike in immigration arrests shows that the administration has continued to advance its mass deportations agenda despite a shift in approach earlier this year from high-profile operations in large American cities that sparked a public outcry to arrests that have garnered less attention but have nonetheless been disruptive.

The July arrest tally of 49,571 marks a 15% jump from 43,021 arrests a month earlier and a 70% increase from 29,241 in February, in the aftermath of the Trump administration's enforcement surge in Minnesota, according to government data that was provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA and analyzed by The Associated Press.

As part of the surging arrest numbers over recent weeks and bolstered by a hiring surge , ICE has made arrests at traffic stops. The agency has increasingly relied on state and local law enforcement partners who are assuming immigration enforcement duties. And ICE officers have started to arrest people from Haiti who've seen their protections from deportation stripped away.

The new arrest numbers show the administration "didn't stop the enforcement," said Mark Krikorian of the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for more immigration restrictions.

"They changed the tactics and are, if anything, being more effective."

State partnerships becoming key to immigration enforcement

Immigration arrests the month before President Donald Trump returned to office hovered a little over 8,000, a figure largely made up of immigrants transferred from city or state jails and prisons and turned over to ICE to remove from the country. During Trump's first year back in office, the numbers started climbing as the administration loosened restrictions on where and whom ICE could arrest while it also infused the agency with billions of dollars.

By December, the number of arrests jumped to more than 40,177, according to the data, which was obtained through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. Homeland Security largely stopped reporting immigration enforcement data at the beginning of the second Trump administration, making the data from the Deportation Data Project one of the few insights into how the agency is operating.

In the aftermath of two fatal shootings in Minnesota in January that sparked protests and an uproar from Democratic lawmakers, arrests began to fall in February. After remaining stagnant for months, the numbers surged in June and then again in July.

The number of arrests made by state and local police departments who partner with ICE has dramatically increased over the last year. Those partnerships, which ICE has grown with the help of generous financial incentives for participating agencies, accounted for 6,500 arrests in July, or about 13% of the total, the data showed. A year earlier, they accounted for less than 5% of ICE's monthly arrests.

Texas and Florida accounted for nearly 20,000 of the July arrests, in a sign of how important those states have become to the Trump administration's mass deportation agenda. Both states have leaned heavily into those cooperation deals with ICE, known as 287g agreements, that allow local and state law enforcement to essentially operate as arms of federal immigration enforcement.

That close cooperation is increasingly resulting in arrests like one last week in Florida's Key West. The manager at the Half Shell Raw Bar said Tuesday that one of his staff members, a 36-year-old asylum seeker who fled Haiti in 2017 after receiving death threats, was arrested by local police and turned over to ICE.

The manager, Bobby Kuchinsky, said the man had worked as a cook and supervisor at the restaurant and was the main provider of his family. Kuchinsky declined to identify the man out of concern for his safety while in custody.

"He was an excellent worker, he learned very fast, he never had any problem with the law," Kuchinsky said in an interview with the AP, noting that it will be a challenge to replace him. "He was a nice kid, he was a family man."

DHS secretary pledged a quieter approach but mass deportations still a priority

In his confirmation hearing earlier this year, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pledged to keep ICE out of the headlines, suggesting that the administration's immigration crackdown might take a softer approach. But his tenure has been marred by a number of fatal shootings of immigrants in encounters with ICE officers. And the figures show Mullin hasn't shifted the agency from Trump's vision for mass deportations.

Under Mullin's predecessor, Kristi Noem, immigration enforcement was often characterized by high-profile operations that targeted specific Democratic cities such as Chicago, Los Angeles and Minneapolis. Operations, often led by former Border Patrol agent Greg Bovino, were blasted out on social media videos showing officers bursting out of moving vans to chase people or rappelling from helicopters onto apartment rooftops.

But Krikorian said those tactics were "provoking a lot of ordinary people, turning them off even if they liked the idea of the immigration law being enforced."

New data shows most immigrants arrested didn't have criminal history

The administration has often said its immigration enforcement operations target people who have committed crimes in the U.S. and as a way to make the country safer.

But the data shows that more than half of those arrested in July had not been convicted of any crimes and were not facing any criminal charges. Less than a quarter of those arrested had been convicted of a crime.

And half of the arrests were non-custodial, which means ICE agents arrested people in the community rather than someone already behind bars or held by local police.

Patricia Quiñonez, a journalist at Utahzolanos, which covers the Venezuelan immigrant community in Utah, said immigration arrests during traffic stops have increased sharply in recent months.

"They stop you for whatever reason — for example, you don't have a driver's license, your vehicle tags are expired, your windows are more tinted than what is allowed. From there, they take advantage of the situation and ask about immigration."

People with valid work permits and pending asylum claims are among those arrested, said Quiñonez, who believes they are being targeted by race.

Salomon reported from Miami, Sullivan from Minneapolis and Foley from Iowa City, Iowa. Associated Press writer Elliot Spagat in San Diego contributed.

articles.title: Dem House hopeful defended music video showing woman restrained, groped and killed
articles.summary: Bobby Pulido defended Gerardo Ortiz's graphic music video depicting sexual violence, adding to controversies as he challenges Monica De La Cruz.
articles.body: In a 2016 interview, Latin Grammy Award-winning artist and Democratic congressional candidate Bobby Pulido defended a fellow singer against criticism for a graphic music video that depicted acts of sexual violence and murder. In the video production of "Fuiste Mía" or "You were mine" by Gerardo Ortiz, a singer walks in on his girlfriend cheating on him. After shooting her lover, he then handcuffs her to a pole, blindfolds her, and gropes her before putting her in the trunk of his car and setting it on fire. In response to backlash, Pulido defended Ortiz, calling the video a matter of artistic direction. "I've made videos with suggestive images; some have stayed, others have been edited, and still others were never used. That's the decision of the artist and their team," Pulido said in response to public backlash for the production. Pulido’s resurfaced response to the music video is the latest in a series of controversies Pulido has tried to downplay as he pursues a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in Texas’ 15th Congressional District — one of the country’s most competitive seats. FORMER DISNEY TEEN STAR EXPOSES CHILLING WARNING SIGNS OF PREDATORY BEHAVIOR IN HOLLYWOOD Pulido is best known for Tejano, or Mexican–Spanish folk-style, songs like "Desvelado" and "Se Murió de Amor," and received five nominations for a Latin Grammy Awards, winning Best Tejano Album in 2025 and 2022. He filed to run for Congress in Texas’ 15th district, challenging Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Texas. A two-term incumbent, she last won election to the district in 2024 in a 57.1% to 42.9% victory over Democratic nominee Michelle Vallejo.  Along the way, Pulido has drawn scrutiny for a resurfaced history of posting links to explicit websites on his personal X account — as well as for a social media post of what appeared to be him urinating on President Donald Trump’s Hollywood Walk of Fame star. Pulido has shrugged off criticism for both, stating in 2024 that it's "it’s impossible to have Twitter and not watch porn," and that he had only poured water on Trump’s star as a joke. More notably, Pulido has also had to fend off criticisms of bringing a registered sex offender to a Texas middle school benefit concert in 2018. DEM TIED TO CARTEL OPERATIVE SAYS 'WHITE NATIONALISTS' JOINING IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT TO 'HUNT DOWN PEOPLE' In that case, Pulido denied knowledge of his associate’s status at the time and has dismissed coverage of it as a "nothing story," according to Axios. Similarly, in his defense of Ortiz, Pulido downplayed the music video, arguing that viewers had become accustomed to increasingly graphic images. "What happens when there's a [car] accident?" Pulido asked, comparing the music video to real-life instances of tragedy. "Traffic doesn't flow because people slow down or even stop to see what happened; something similar happens with the regional Mexican genre when these kinds of incidents occur." At least one Republican onlooker is left unconvinced by the defense of the music video — and defenses of other past behaviors. "Bobby Pulido has spent his entire adult life defending perverts and predators while lashing out at members of law enforcement who keep Texans safe. He is a truly sick individual who is morally rotten," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital. DEM RIPPED FOR ‘DISGUSTING’ ABSENCE ON BILL TO PUNISH VIOLENT CRIMINALS AFTER GIRL STRANGLED IN GRISLY KILLING CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Pulido campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment about his defense of the video and whether he had a track record of downplaying potentially problematic conduct.

articles.title: Mike Lindell misses deadline for recount payment, seeks restraining order
articles.summary: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell (R) announced Monday he will file a temporary restraining order against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon amid his ongoi...
articles.body:
MyPillow founder Mike Lindell (R) announced Monday he will file a temporary restraining order against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon amid his ongoing efforts to fund a private recount of the state's gubernatorial primaries.

His campaign said in a statement that Simon's office had put Lindell "in an untenable position" by placing restrictions on his proposed audit — limiting the recount to just the two leading Republican candidates.

Lindell lost the election to Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) by roughly 11 percentage points, according to Decision Desk HQ. But the MyPillow founder refused to concede, later claiming there were irregularities in vote totals .

"The rest of the candidates' vote would not be counted under their contingent plan. Nor would the Democrat ballots be recounted," Lindell's campaign wrote Monday.

"Why is this important?" it continued. "In addition to being a violation of Minnesota state law, the anomalies on election night reporting identified by Mike Lindell's team show an algorithm that applies to ALL of the candidates not simply Lindell and Demuth."

Cassondra Knudson, a spokesperson for Simon, told The Hill that the office did not receive a payment or a discretionary request by the Aug. 24 deadline. She added that, at this time, the state does not plan to conduct a recount for the Aug. 11 primary.

In its statement, Lindell's campaign attached an authorization form appearing to show an $825,000 transaction in progress as proof of "wire transfer readiness" for the potential audit, dated Monday morning.

The campaign is now asking the state officials to waive the Monday deadline until a court can rule on the alleged Minnesota law violations.

Knudson said that "next steps" for Lindell's legal action against Simon and the Minnesota State Canvassing Board for their handling of the recount processes "will be decided by the court."

"Our office provided the contingent recount plan to Mr. Lindell after it was approved by the State Canvassing Board on August 18. The plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures and is consistent with previous recount plans," she said.

The MyPillow founder currently owes the electronic voting system company Smartmatic $56,369 in sanctions following a defamation lawsuit — which his attorneys say he cannot afford. Lindell accused the company in several media appearances of rigging the 2020 presidential election, echoing President Trump's similar false claims .

On Aug. 19, Lindell's lawyers sent a letter to U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan to file a motion to reconsider the ruling holding him liable for defamation.

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW has mentioned Trump aide Natalie Harp hundreds of times since Ossoff's viral jab
articles.summary: Natalie Harp's name was mentioned over 700 times on CNN and MS NOW over the past several days after Jon Ossoff's viral stump speech sparked a firestorm.
articles.body: CNN and MS NOW have gone wall-to-wall covering one of President Donald Trump's most trusted aides. Natalie Harp was dragged into a political firestorm after being name-dropped in a viral stump speech by Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who appeared to suggest that she and Trump had an inappropriate relationship — though Ossoff has attempted to distance himself from the innuendo. Now more than one week removed from Ossoff's comment, the liberal news networks have gone into overdrive with their fixation on the 35-year-old White House staffer. JON OSSOFF'S CONTROVERSIAL TRUMP JAB SPARKS MEDIA FEEDING FRENZY OVER WHITE HOUSE AIDE NATALIE HARP Between last Monday through last Sunday, Harp's name was mentioned at least 308 times on CNN and a whopping 344 times on MS NOW within the seven-day period, according to Grabien transcripts. That relentless coverage of Harp continued this week. CNN's mentions of Harp have ticked up to 318, while MS NOW has surpassed 400 mentions through mid-Tuesday. Both networks gave breathless attention to reports of the letters Harp had written to Trump expressing staunch loyalty and how she was within Trump's tight-knit circle who joined him on his secret plane switch out of Turkey last month. CNN FIRES BACK AT TRUMP WHITE HOUSE OVER ATTACKS ON REPORTER, CALLS THEM 'BENEATH THE OFFICE' MS NOW reported how Harp doesn't have a security clearance despite her close access to the president, while CNN dug up old social media posts showing her "zealous" support for Trump on Jan. 6.  CNN previously reported, citing unnamed sources, that Harp allegedly "jumped into an SUV trunk" to ride with Trump for an October 2023 court appearance because she "wouldn’t take no for an answer" when the vehicle didn't have enough room. CNN also drew intense backlash among conservatives for interviewing Harp's estranged brother, Preston Harp, on air. WHITE HOUSE TEARS INTO OSSOFF WITH BRUTAL TAKEDOWN AFTER JAB AT KEY TRUMP AIDE: ‘LIGHTWEIGHT LOSER’ Additionally, the White House sharply admonished CNN White House correspondent Kristen Holmes for asking Trump about Ossoff's comment, prompting CNN's fiery response in defense of its reporter, calling the attacks against her "beneath the office." Curtis Houck, the managing editor of NewsBusters of the conservative watchdog Media Research Center, told Fox News Digital that CNN and MS NOW have "gone full bore" on Harp because of their vehement opposition to Trump. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "They're more than willing to invoke someone else and drag their name through the mud," Houck said. "And I think it's really sick and disgusting." Representatives for CNN and MS NOW did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Pro-life CEO predicts Trump FDA nominee could bring renewed scrutiny to abortion drug risks
articles.summary: Trump's FDA nominee Heidi Overton could bring renewed scrutiny to mifepristone, says Americans United for Life CEO who calls her a "pro-life" pick.
articles.body: The chief executive of America's oldest pro-life organization told Fox News Digital that President Donald Trump's FDA nominee, Dr. Heidi Overton, could bring renewed scrutiny to mifepristone, the abortion drug at the center of an ongoing federal safety review. John Mize, CEO of Americans United for Life (AUL), said he has had five or six conversations with Overton, who is known for her pro-life views. She currently serves as Trump's deputy assistant for domestic policy. "I think she's going to bring objectivity to the issue of mifepristone in a way that will expose this drug for the damage it causes women," Mize said in an interview on Friday, adding that his organization is "optimistic" that Overton will be a "pro-life FDA commissioner." Overton's nomination comes just weeks after an 18-year-old woman in North Carolina was accused of using mifepristone and misoprostol to terminate a pregnancy at 31 weeks, well beyond mifepristone's FDA-approved limit of 10 weeks. HAWLEY INTRODUCES BILL TO STRIP FDA APPROVAL FROM 'INHERENTLY DANGEROUS' ABORTION PILL Mize has led AUL for two-and-a-half years, but the nonprofit has advocated against abortion, euthanasia, assisted suicide and other practices it considers threats to human life since its founding in 1971. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255). Mize said he believes Overton is the "right candidate" to lead the FDA, citing her experience in government, clinical medicine and medical research. If confirmed, Overton would take the reins of the agency responsible for regulating abortion medication, including mifepristone. Mifepristone carries an FDA boxed warning, the agency’s strongest safety warning, for the risk of serious and sometimes fatal infections or bleeding. Prompted initially by COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, the FDA stopped enforcing the drug's in-person dispensing requirement in 2021 and later removed it permanently after reviewing the available safety data. Under current FDA rules, patients do not necessarily have to see a physician in person before receiving a prescription, allowing mifepristone to be prescribed after telehealth visit and mailed by a certified pharmacy. Mize wants those rules tightened. SUPREME COURT TEMPORARILY BLOCKS APPEALS COURT RULING ON ABORTION PILL, RESTORES WIDER ACCESS TO DRUG "Dr. Overton and I share a very similar perspective that the drug is dangerous, particularly in an unregulated way for women," Mize told Fox News Digital. "I firmly believe she understands the clinical implications of taking a drug with a black box warning and now shipping it in the mail." Overton has publicly criticized mifepristone and other abortion drugs, which accounted for about 65% of clinician-provided abortions in 2023, according to the Guttmacher Institute, up from 53% in 2020 before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. In a February 2023 policy brief for the America First Policy Institute, a MAGA-aligned think tank where she previously served as chief policy officer, Overton denounced federal policymakers for expanding access to abortion pills. She also accused the Biden administration of using the COVID-19 pandemic to wrongly justify allowing mifepristone and misoprostol, a drug that induces early labor, to be sent to patients through the mail. FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS Taken together, the two drugs terminate early pregnancies: mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed to sustain the pregnancy, while misoprostol causes contractions that expel the fetus. "Abortion is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly because it devalues and extinguishes innocent human life," she wrote at the time. "America First policies should focus on immediately halting the effort to normalize abortion-on-demand and on broadly recognizing the evidence of the risk posed to women." Mize pointed to a 2025 study by the Ethics and Public Policy Center, a conservative think tank, that analyzed insurance claims from 865,727 mifepristone abortions between 2017 and 2023 and found a serious adverse event rate of nearly 11%. This included conditions such as hemorrhaging, sepsis or infection. The study received immediate pushback, with the medical community saying it used a flawed methodology. The paper was also not peer-reviewed or published in a medical journal, factors Mize said Overton is aware of. HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS "It's not the whole picture, and Dr. Overton would say that," Mize said. "But it's an important indicator as to what's happening in the real world. So I believe she will do a really good job of evaluating the study." Mize said he hopes Overton will impose tighter restrictions on mifepristone after reviewing the evidence, potentially restoring a requirement that women see a doctor in person before receiving a prescription. He described Overton as "measured" and "methodical" while cautioning that pro-life advocates should not expect her to pursue immediate, sweeping changes at the FDA. "I don't get the sense that she's gonna move quickly on issues," Mize said. SUPREME COURT KEEPS BROADER ACCESS TO ABORTION PILL MIFEPRISTONE IN PLACE WHILE LEGAL FIGHT CONTINUES Dr. Marty Makary, the previous FDA commissioner, resigned in May after clashing with Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers. He also drew criticism from pro-life activists, who accused the agency under his leadership of slow-walking its safety review of mifepristone. If confirmed, Overton would inherit the review, which was formally announced in September 2025 and does not have a scheduled completion date. The FDA has noted these types of studies typically take a year or longer to conduct. After that review is completed, Mize said the next step for Overton, ideally, would be "a longer term, deep dive evaluation on this medication to determine if it should even be on the market." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Mize acknowledged that not all the evidence is in yet but made clear that his preference would be to take mifepristone off the market. "From my perspective, any medication that denies someone the opportunity to live and kills a human being shouldn't be something that we're promoting amongst the FDA," Mize said. "Ultimately, I would love to see this drug removed from the market for those reasons. Culturally, we might not be there right now." Overton’s confirmation hearing has not yet been scheduled but is expected to take place after the Senate returns from its summer recess on Sept. 14.
