articles.title: Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’
articles.summary: The Republican Senate candidate announced the plan with a graphic flagged as ‘Made with AI’
articles.body:
Ken Paxton , a Republican candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has unveiled plans to tackle the "negative impact" of datacenters amid a growing backlash across the political spectrum.

Paxton, endorsed by Donald Trump but facing a close contest against Democrat James Talarico, posted a "Texas first" datacenter plan on X with a graphic that the social media network flagged as "Made with AI".

Republicans have been struggling to keep up with a shift in public opinion fueled by concerns that power- and water-hungry datacenters will push up energy costs and harm the environment. Some fear the issue could prove costly in November's US midterm elections.

Related: Hakeem Jeffries defends his meeting with Trump envoy Jared Kushner

An Annenberg Public Policy Center survey last month found that 61% of Americans now oppose the building of a new datacenter in their area, an increase from 49% in March. This includes 69% of Democrats, 54% of Republicans and 53% of independents.

Last year Greg Abbott , the governor of Texas, dubbed his state the "epicenter of AI development", but on Sunday he told ABC's This Week program that tech companies "basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them and that's why they got the backlash they deserve".

On Monday his ally Paxton, currently the state attorney general in Texas, outlined a four-point plan that includes banning Chinese technology to power US datacenters, holding companies criminally liable if AI chatbots undermine children's safety and cutting red tape to ensure datacenters do not raise Texans' electricity bills.

He also pledged to support Abbott's state plan to ban new datacenters from rural neighborhoods, repeal sales tax exemptions and ensure they are adding to Texas's electricity capacity rather than taking from it.

Paxton said in a statement: "Texans deserve a fighter to lead and represent them as we address the growing presence of datacenters in Texas and stop their negative impact on our neighborhoods.

"This plan will ensure that happens while putting Texas first, protecting our culture and land, and safeguarding our families and communities. My plan will also work to ensure that datacenters are not utilized to power Al platforms that endanger our children."

The move signals an effort by Paxton, a rightwing populist who defeated the incumbent US senator John Cornyn in a Republican primary runoff , to blunt attacks on what could be a potential electoral issue. His rival Talarico has urged tighter regulations on datacenter development and an end to sweetheart tax deals for big tech companies.

Talarico accused Paxton of trying to erase his history giving datacenter tax handouts. He said in a statement: "Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million dollars from the datacenter industry, voted to flood Texas with datacenters by giving them billions in tax handouts, and has refused to use his power as attorney general to respond to Texans' requests to block datacenter development in their communities.

"Now he's scared his ties to big datacenter companies will lose him the election, so he's making a sad attempt to reverse course by releasing a plan he literally used AI to make."

The race is tight in what is traditionally a Republican stronghold. A Fox News poll in late July showed Talarico leading 51% to 48%. The Cook Political Report describes the election as a toss-up .

Paxton is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate . He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pretrial diversion agreement. Last year his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce " on biblical grounds ", citing adultery.

Politicians are scrambling to adjust to the backlash against AI datacenters, which consume huge quantities of electricity and water, threaten to alter the landscape of local communities, and create relatively few jobs.

Josh Shapiro, the Democratic governor of Pennsylvania, last year championed a $20bn investment by Amazon but last week signed an executive order he said imposes the "strictest guardrails in the nation". Bernie Sanders, an independent senator for Vermont, has urged big tech leaders to pause AI development.

The Axios website reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned leading AI companies that voter discontent with the centers is endangering the party's chances of defending a Senate seat in Ohio.

Trump, however, remains supportive of the industry. He told Punchbowl News recently: "I saw Texas the other day sort of is against datacenters. I think it's a mistake. And I'm not taking positions, I just think it's a mistake, because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community."

articles.title: Antisemitic streamer finally makes Dem leader snap with rare rebuke: ‘Malicious’
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries calls Hasan Piker's claim that Jewish Americans invite violence against themselves dangerous and antisemitic.
articles.body: House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York is slamming comments from Hasan Piker after the far-left controversial online streamer suggested that Jewish Americans were inviting violence against themselves over their support for Israel. "The malicious claim that American Jews are inviting violence against themselves is dangerous and antisemitic," Jeffries charged in a social media post. And he added in a CNN interview on Tuesday that Piker's comments were "malicious" and "should not be tolerated by anyone in the public square." While Jeffries became the highest-ranking congressional Democrat to fire back at Piker, the criticism from the top Democrat in the U.S. House comes after he has largely stayed silent on the far-left insurgency, backed in part by Piker, that's gripped his party this election cycle. Jeffries spoke out after Piker, on his stream last week, featured an image of state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee in Michigan's 11th Congressional District. Moss, who is Jewish, has said that people are sharing a fake audio clip of him claiming that his entire reason for running for Congress is to make sure that America continues to support Israel. EL-SAYED TRIES TO DISTANCE HIMSELF FROM HASAN PIKER AFTER LATEST FIRESTORM "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker warned. Piker, who has over three million online followers, has repeatedly stood by his numerous past comments slamming Israel over its ongoing war against Hamas in Gaza. Jeffries emphasized in his social media post, "There is zero justification for threats against the safety of our Jewish brothers and sisters at a moment of rising hate. We will fight the cancer of antisemitism with the fierce urgency of now." ABDUL EL-SAYED FACES OFF WTIH FOX NEWS' JESSE WATTERS IN PRIMETIME Piker's comments were also blasted by Democratic Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., who charged that Piker is "a hack who thrives on hate." Rep. Susie Lee, D-Nev., took to X to write, "Claims that American Jews are responsible for the violence being committed against their communities are unacceptable and cannot be tolerated. It’s dangerous and antisemitic." "We must stand up to the scourge of antisemitism wherever it rears its ugly head," Lee added. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., praised Jeffries' pushback against Piker. In an interview on Fox News' "America's Newsroom," Gottheimer called Piker's comments something "right out of the Nazi playbook." Gottheimer, who is Jewish and a strong supporter of Israel, emphasized, "This is a call for violence against Jews," He was also critical of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan. DEMOCRATS 'WHO NEVER VOTED REPUBLICAN' BACKING THIS GOP SENATE NOMINEE El-Sayed, who is facing off against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in battleground Michigan in a high-stakes Senate showdown, on Monday tried to put some distance between himself and Piker, who is a top supporter. "I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople," El-Sayed said in a statement. Gottheimer said that El-Sayed insufficiently pushed back against Piker: "El-Sayed's response was pathetic," "No Democratic members should allow Piker anywhere near them on the campaign trail," Gottheimer argued. Piker endorsed El-Sayed for the Democratic nomination and appeared at some of the candidate's campaign events including a primary night party earlier this month in Detroit, Michigan. Piker's latest comments were blasted by a growing number of Republicans since they grabbed attention this past weekend, including Rogers, who took aim at both Piker and El-Sayed in a social media post. "More calls for violence coming out of the El-Sayed campaign," Rogers said on Sunday. And he claimed, "Here is his running mate, Hasan Piker, saying that if AMERICAN JEWS support Israel, they will be violently targeted because of it." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Rogers, who is making a major push to court Democrats in Michigan, added, "Absolutely DISGUSTING. If Abdul El-Sayed had any courage at all, he would call this out and disavow Hasan Piker once and for all. We’re waiting, Abdul…" El-Sayed, in his Monday statement, wrote, "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past." "My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters. Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk," he added. WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW A former Wayne County Health Department director, El-Sayed, if elected in November, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. The epidemiologist who unsuccessfully ran for governor as an insurgent candidate in 2018 has made support for Medicare for all a major component of his campaign and has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP El-Sayed used the word "bloodthirsty" to characterize Israel's military moves in Gaza in an MS NOW interview this month and accused Israeli leadership of genocide against Palestinians. He has argued against unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel, as have other progressive politicians. And El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to directly answer whether Israel has the right to exist. But El-Sayed has also repeatedly stated that he stands "in solidarity with my Jewish sisters and brothers" to "condemn antisemitism."

articles.title: El-Sayed's defense of Sharia Law stance sparks online eruption from Christians, conservatives: 'He's done'
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's comparison of Sharia law to Catholic canon law during his Jesse Watters interview ignited fierce pushback from conservative commentators.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed sparked controversy on social media Monday night after comparing Sharia law to Christian canon law during an interview with Fox News anchor Jesse Watters. "Getting rid of Sharia law is White supremacy?" Watters said to El-Sayed, bringing up past comments from the Michigan candidate opposing a ban on Sharia law and comparing those efforts to white supremacy. "Can you explain that one?" Sayed responded by comparing Sharia, Islamic law based on religious texts, to Catholic Church law and governance. "Nobody is trying to push Sharia law on anyone else, just like I hope nobody is trying to push Canon law on anybody else, because we live in an America where you should have the freedom of your religion," El-Sayed said. TRUMP INAUGURATION PASTOR SAYS DEARBORN CHRISTIANS 'AFRAID' TO SPEAK OUT IN MUSLIM-MAJORITY CITY The comparison sparked pushback on social media from users highlighting the differences between the two viewpoints and traditions. "He lies and says no one is trying to push Sharia (they are), and draws a false equivalency to Christian Canon law," Charlie Kirk Show Executive Producer Andrew Kolvet posted on X. "Canon law determines how Christian leaders, churches, and Christians should live, but Canon law is limited to affairs of the Church (spiritual penalties). Canon law grants great autonomy to the state." Kolvet continued, "Sharia law is MUCH more comprehensive, governing all aspects of life, and historically, and according to many contemporary Islamic clerics, dictates the affairs of the state." EL-SAYED'S AGENDA PUTS ‘PERMANENTLY’ CHANGED AMERICA ON THE LINE IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE, GOP FIREBRAND WARNS "Sharia law is incompatible with Western Civilization," political commentator Carl Jackson posted on X. "I’m tired of El-Sayed playing the victim card in attempt to avoid legitimate scrutiny of Islam." "Yeah, it’s over for him," Fox News contributor Kaylee McGhee White posted on X. "Rogers by 6." "@AbdulElSayed doesn’t get to bloviate about sharia being a mere ‘practice’ of faith when it’s Islamic jurisprudence used to supplant western jurisprudence," conservative commentator and radio host Dana Loesch posted on X. "'Jesse, the Catholic Church requires ministers to use plant oils in sacraments with the blessings of a bishop, so why shouldn't courts allow Muslim men to have four wives?'" conservative commentator Michael Knowles posted on X. "Canon law applies to Catholics," conservative commentator Pamela Geller posted on X. "There is no compulsion is Canon law. Jewish law applies only to Jews. There is no compulsion in Jewish law. It is voluntary. The sharia is a comprehensive legal system governing every aspect of human life, and asserts authority over non-Muslims." "This was a very strange prepared defense from Abdul," GOP communicator Matt Whitlock posted on X. "I expected him to say it was out of context, not reflective of current views, etc. Instead he accepted the premise and defended promoting Sharia Law - opening that lane up to more attacks." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the El-Sayed campaign for comment. Abdul El-Sayed previously said he felt religiously obligated to follow Sharia-compliant practices in a 2009 interview with The New York Times. "Ultimately, the question is, when I die and I stand before God and go through everything I did in my life, I don’t want to say I did it the easy way instead of the Shariah-compliant way," El-Sayed told the Times. "Not because of fear but because of obligation." Sharia law traditionally prescribed death for people who leave Islam, placed strict restrictions on what women can do and allowed child marriage. El-Sayed has spoken out against bans on Sharia law, arguing such efforts are rooted in White supremacy. "The state of Oklahoma voted in a referendum to amend the constitution to ban Shariah law. What does that mean? I don’t know. And yet the voters banned it anyway," he said in 2022. "The same exact forces that drove Native peoples from their land two centuries ago, destroyed Black Wall Street a century ago, bombed a building decades ago and tried to ban Sharia law not a decade ago, those forces are alive and well today. "The reason I wanted to go all the way back to the 1830s is because you can’t understand a Sharia ban without understanding the Trail of Tears. You can’t understand the efforts to uproot Muslim Americans without understanding the Tulsa massacre. You cannot understand the challenges we face today without understanding white supremacy." Fox News Digital’s Robert Schmad contributed to this report

articles.title: Pritzker’s swagger stunt backfires as critics roast viral video: ‘Cringiest thing he’s ever posted’
articles.summary: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker's black-and-white "aura-farming" video drew widespread mockery on social media, with critics targeting his weight and taxes.
articles.body: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker showed off his swagger in a tongue-in-cheek social media video Monday, prompting a wave of mockery from critics online. The video, recorded in black and white and notching more than 1 million views, features Pritzker making a variety of model-like expressions at the camera behind a caption that reads "when you’re in an aura-farming contest and your opponent in JB." Aura-farming is a common piece of slang used to describe the taking of certain actions with the explicit goal of acquiring swag. Many social media users did not agree with Pritzker’s assessment of himself. PROGRESSIVE MINNEAPOLIS MAYOR'S VIRAL HIP-HOP MOVES SPARK 'HUMILIATION RITUAL' MOCKERY ONLINE "Only thing bigger than the ratio this tweet is getting is…well," White House deputy assistant to the president Kaelan Dorr posted in response to the video. "Pritzker is kind of a medical marvel," conservative commentator Matt Walsh wrote. "He looks gaunt and frail from Ozempic and also still morbidly obese at the exact same time. He's taking the concept of ‘skinny fat’ to places never thought possible." WHITE HOUSE FIRES BACK AFTER 'SLOB' JB PRITZKER SAYS TRUMP IS SUFFERING FROM 'DEMENTIA' Pritzker wrote the phrase "governor-maxxing" alongside his video on X. "Maxxing" as a suffix denotes that someone is doing something in a highly optimized way. "Looks-maxxing," for instance, refers to the act of taking one's appearance, physical fitness, and demeanor seriously as to maximize attractiveness. Some on social media used the governor’s phrasing to poke fun at him. Brian Costin, who is a high-level staffer at a right-of-center advocacy group in Illinois, accused Pritzker of "property-tax-maxxing," "state-and-local-tax-burden-maxxing," "cell-phone-tax-maxxing," "gas-tax-hike-maxxing," and "blaming-everyone-else-maxxing," among other things. Others focused on his weight, claiming that Pritzker was "buffet-maxxing" or "waistline-maxxing." REPUBLICANS RIP 4 BLUE STATES FOR KEEPING TAXES ON TIPS, OVERTIME AFTER TRUMP REPRIEVE "When you’re a grown nepo-kid and believe you’re as impressive as the people you’re paying say you are," Fox Business anchor David Asman said of Pritzker, whose father, Donald Pritzker, helped build the Hyatt hotel chain with his brother Jay. Pritzker has a history of making widely mocked social media posts, including his frequent attempts to spar with the president. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Might be the cringiest thing he's ever posted, and that is saying a lot," RealClearPolitics president Tom Bevan wrote. Pritzker's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Live election results: Darline Graham, Ralph Norman face off in SC Senate
articles.summary: Sen. Darline Graham, a political newcomer, was slammed after being stumped by a basic foreign policy question. She faces Rep. Ralph Norman on Tuesday.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is once again putting his credibility in Republican primaries on the line, this time for South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham in what could be his riskiest bet of the 2026 midterm primary season. Polls have closed in the Palmetto State at 7 p.m. ET in the closely watched runoff between Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman after neither won a majority in a special election earlier in August.

The president last week stopped in Myrtle Beach to campaign on behalf of the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed to finish her brother's term at Trump's behest.

"This is the easiest race that I've ever seen," Trump said during the rally. "We have a great candidate."

President Trump visits Myrtle Beach to campaign for Graham, see photos

But after Trump scored an almost perfect primary endorsement record earlier this year, Republican voters have rejected his choices in gubernatorial primaries in Minnesota, Iowa and Georgia, and for House races in Florida. Graham may be vulnerable after admitting she is "not that informed on national security," in a debate with Norman.

Voters in Oklahoma are also heading to the polls in runoff races for governor and the U.S. Senate , where there is a contest to fill the seat formerly held by current Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

08:46 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

Everton Blair has defeated Marcye Scott to complete the term of her father, the late Rep. David Scott.

The Associated Press and Decision Desk HQ called the race for the former Gwinnett County Board of Education chair at 8:38 p.m. ET and 8:41 p.m. ET, respectively.

Norman is a five-term congressman, largely unknown outside the Palmetto State, who drew support from former Gov. Nikki Haley, former Gov. Mark Sanford and controversial outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace. He placed third in a Republican gubernatorial primary in June.

Norman first served in the South Carolina House of Representatives from 2005 to 2006 and again from 2009 to 2017 after working for his family's well-known commercial real estate development company, the Warren Norman Company, which was founded by his father.

He was then elected to serve the state's 5th District in Congress in 2017. The father-of-four adult kids and his wife of 51 years, Elaine Rice Norman, live in his hometown of Rock Hill, South Carolina near the North Carolina border.

08:00 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

Polls closed for the Oklahoma Democratic Senate primary runoff and Republican gubernatorial runoff at 8 p.m. ET. Results are expected shortly.

The polls in Georgia's special election runoff for the U.S. House closed at 7 p.m. ET. Results are expected shortly.

07:00 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

The polls for the South Carolina special Senate Republican runoff closed at 7 p.m. ET. Results are expected shortly.

Who is Darline Graham? Here's what to know

06:30 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel and Saman Shafiq

Darline Graham is the first woman to represent the state of South Carolina in the Senate after being appointed to the seat in the wake of her brother Lindsey Graham's death in July. Tuesday's primary will determine if she has a chance to become the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate by the state.

She grew up in Central, in the Midlands of South Carolina, with her brother and parents, who owned a pool hall, bar and restaurant.

The two faced hardship early on after their parents' deaths within a year of one another. Their mother died in 1976 of Hodgkin's lymphoma, and 15 months later, their father died of a heart attack, USA TODAY previously reported .

She was 13 years old when her father died, and Lindsey Graham raised his sister after their parents' deaths. In a 2015 interview with The New York Times , Graham described her brother as "kind of like a brother, a father and a mother rolled into one."

Graham is married to Larry Nordone, has two daughters and holds a master's degree in rehabilitation counseling.

Before actively taking part in politics, Graham worked in disability services and workforce development, USA TODAY previously reported .

Graham currently serves on the South Carolina State Workforce Development Board and is president-elect of the National Council of State Agencies for the Blind.

For nearly seven years, she also served as a commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, where she focused on helping blind and low-vision people achieve employment, independence and economic self-sufficiency.

Who is facing off in the Oklahoma gubernatorial primary?

05:38 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond is set to face off against Trump-backed former state lawmaker Mike Mazzei in Tuesday's GOP gubernatorial runoff.

Each candidate got around 26% in the June primary.

Drummond saw big-name Oklahomans , including Clay Bennett, Greg Love and Barry Switzer, contribute to his campaign, while Mazzei drew financial support from term-limited Gov. Kevin Stitt and Stitt's inner circle.

The winner will face Democrat Cyndi Munson in November.

Georgia runoff to replace David Scott will test another family's legacy

A special election to replace longtime Georgia Rep. David Scott, a Democrat from the Atlanta Metro area who died in April, is being held in his district on Tuesday. Scott was the first Black chairman of the powerful House Agriculture Committee.

No candidate in the July election garnered the 50% total needed to avoid a runoff race. His daughter, Marcye Scott, and Everton Blair, the former Gwinnett County Board of Education chair, were the top two finishers in July. They advanced to the Aug. 25 runoff.

The winner will complete the final months of Scott's term but will not appear on the November ballot to win a full term. Blair previously lost a competitive House primary race for a full term to state Rep. Jasmine Clark. That primary field also included Bravo reality TV star Heavenly Kimes.

05:18 PM ET, August 25 2026, Phillip M. Bailey

Underscoring Sen. Darline Graham's importance to the administration, President Donald Trump's super PAC made a rare withdrawal from its massive campaign treasure chest on her behalf ahead of the South Carolina runoff.

Federal Election Commission records show MAGA Inc. spent roughly $830,000 on phone banking and text alerts aimed at reminding voters about the political neophyte's bid against Rep. Ralph Norman.

That last-minute expenditure is notable given that Trump's super PAC has mostly stayed out of other battleground primary contests despite sitting on a massive amount of money. It has raked in more than $403 million , mostly from billionaires and other successful business owners.

The only other time MAGA Inc. has doled out campaign cash this year was about $18,000 for Republican Clay Fuller, who won the Georgia special election to fill the seat vacated by former Rep. Majorie Taylor Greene.

"The president is going to expend substantial resources to win the midterms," James Blair, a former White House aide who now runs MAGA Inc., told former press secretary Sean Spicer in June. "He cares deeply about the party winning and anything he can do to support that he's going to do."

Poll shows Graham, Norman in virtual tie in 'toss-up' race

05:03 PM ET, August 25 2026, Terry Collins

The latest polling on the South Carolina Republican Senate runoff between Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman on Aug. 25 indicates a potentially closer race than expected.

A tracking poll from the Atlanta-based Trafalgar Group shows a tie between Graham and Norman at almost 48%, only adding to the intrigue. The poll of 1,027 registered voters conducted Aug. 22-24 has a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points.

A similar poll conducted two weeks ago saw Graham ahead of Norman at 26.4% to 19.5%. That poll was taken before Graham's gaffe when she was asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are important U.S. national security interests during an Aug. 18 debate . Many political experts believe Graham's answer was a gaffe that exposed her political inexperience compared with the more seasoned Norman.

"I honestly have no real clue what's going to happen," Danielle Vinson , a politics and international affairs professor at Furman University, told USA TODAY. "Can (Graham) win the sentimentality vote and her loyalty to Trump carry her, or will voters want something different? This race is definitely a toss-up for sure."

Rep. Nancy Mace endorses Norman for SC Senate

04:48 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire

South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mance endorsed her House colleague Tuesday over Sen. Darline Graham, who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump.

"It's been nearly twenty years since South Carolina has had an open U.S. Senate seat. Today, we don't crown a leader. We elect one," she wrote on social media . "Ralph Norman is the only candidate with a 100% conservative voting record. He is tried and true. He never backs down."

Once closely aligned with Trump, Mace has been distanced from the president over her push to release the Jeffrey Epstein files. Trump went on the endorse Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette over Mace in the 2026 South Carolina gubernatorial primary.

04:20 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel

Sen. Darline Graham spoke to reporters after casting her vote in Lexington, South Carolina.

She said that she was "looking forward" to the runoff results and is "confident" that she will win the nomination to take the place of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, her brother, on the Republican ballot line in November.

Her race against Rep. Ralph Northam is a test of President Trump's sway in the Republican party, especially in the wake of the ongoing U.S. war in Iran as the conflict nears its six-month mark. Recent primaries have seen some Trump-backed candidates lose in surprising upsets.

04:05 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire

The Department of Justice is monitoring polls in Charleston County, South Carolina, it announced Tuesday .

The monitors include four Civil Rights Division attorneys, one South Carolina assistant U.S. attorney and one staff employee with the South Carolina U.S. Attorney's Office.

Poll monitoring is a routine responsibility of the DOJ that has occurred under Democratic and Republican administrations.

The department has sent more than 80 people to seven states and more than 200 locations to monitor polling sites during this year's primary election cycle, it said. Monitors were recently deployed to Michigan and Minnesota, for example.

04:04 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire

In Oklahoma's Democratic Senate primary runoff, democratic socialist nurse N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas and minister Jim Priest will face off, continuing the in-fighting about the future shape of the Democratic party.

Also in Georgia today, the late Rep. David Scott's daughter, Marcye Scott, and former Gwinnett County School Board Chairman Everton Blair will square off in a special election to fill the remaining months of the congressman's seat.

The only other time MAGA Inc. has doled out campaign cash this year was about $18,000 for Republican Clay Fuller, who won the Georgia special election to fill the seat vacated by former Rep. Majorie Taylor Greene.

"The president is going to expend substantial resources to win the midterms," James Blair, a former White House aide who now runs MAGA Inc., told former press secretary Sean Spicer in June. "He cares deeply about the party winning and anything he can do to support that he's going to do."
Poll shows Graham, Norman in virtual tie in 'toss-up' race
05:03 PM ET, August 25 2026, Terry Collins
The latest polling on the South Carolina Republican Senate runoff between Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman on Aug. 25 indicates a potentially closer race than expected.

A tracking poll from the Atlanta-based Trafalgar Group shows a tie between Graham and Norman at almost 48%, only adding to the intrigue. The poll of 1,027 registered voters conducted Aug. 22-24 has a margin of error of 2.9 percentage points.

A similar poll conducted two weeks ago saw Graham ahead of Norman at 26.4% to 19.5%. That poll was taken before Graham's gaffe when she was asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are important U.S. national security interests during an Aug. 18 debate . Many political experts believe Graham's answer was a gaffe that exposed her political inexperience compared with the more seasoned Norman.

"I honestly have no real clue what's going to happen," Danielle Vinson , a politics and international affairs professor at Furman University, told USA TODAY. "Can (Graham) win the sentimentality vote and her loyalty to Trump carry her, or will voters want something different? This race is definitely a toss-up for sure."
Rep. Nancy Mace endorses Norman for SC Senate
04:48 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire
South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mance endorsed her House colleague Tuesday over Sen. Darline Graham, who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump.

"It's been nearly twenty years since South Carolina has had an open U.S. Senate seat. Today, we don't crown a leader. We elect one," she wrote on social media . "Ralph Norman is the only candidate with a 100% conservative voting record. He is tried and true. He never backs down."

Once closely aligned with Trump, Mace has been distanced from the president over her push to release the Jeffrey Epstein files. Trump went on the endorse Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette over Mace in the 2026 South Carolina gubernatorial primary.
04:20 PM ET, August 25 2026, James Powel
Sen. Darline Graham spoke to reporters after casting her vote in Lexington, South Carolina.

She said that she was "looking forward" to the runoff results and is "confident" that she will win the nomination to take the place of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, her brother, on the Republican ballot line in November.

Her race against Rep. Ralph Northam is a test of President Trump's sway in the Republican party, especially in the wake of the ongoing U.S. war in Iran as the conflict nears its six-month mark. Recent primaries have seen some Trump-backed candidates lose in surprising upsets.
04:05 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire
The Department of Justice is monitoring polls in Charleston County, South Carolina, it announced Tuesday .
The monitors include four Civil Rights Division attorneys, one South Carolina assistant U.S. attorney and one staff employee with the South Carolina U.S. Attorney's Office.
Poll monitoring is a routine responsibility of the DOJ that has occurred under Democratic and Republican administrations.

The department has sent more than 80 people to seven states and more than 200 locations to monitor polling sites during this year's primary election cycle, it said. Monitors were recently deployed to Michigan and Minnesota, for example.
04:04 PM ET, August 25 2026, Sarah D. Wire

In Oklahoma's Democratic Senate primary runoff, democratic socialist nurse N'Kiyla Jasmine Thomas and minister Jim Priest will face off, continuing the in-fighting about the future shape of the Democratic party.

Also in Georgia today, the late Rep. David Scott's daughter, Marcye Scott, and former Gwinnett County School Board Chairman Everton Blair will square off in a special election to fill the remaining months of the congressman's seat.

articles.title: Secret Service aware of Iranian video threat targeting Barron Trump, agency says
articles.summary: A video aired on Iranian state media depicts locations tied to Barron Trump and offers a suggested $10 million reward for his exact location.
articles.body: The U.S. Secret Service said it was aware of a video aired on Iranian state media threatening President Trump's youngest son, Barron Trump. "The U.S. Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees," Nate Herring, a Secret Service spokesperson, told Fox News Digital. "Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence," Herring added. TRUMP HAS BECOME AMERICA'S MOST TARGETED LEADER, FACING THREATS EVERY FEW MONTHS The video depicts locations associated with the younger Trump's whereabouts. It ends with a suggested $10 million reward for his location. Iranian state media has aired content on multiple occasions threatening Trump and his family following the assassination of Iran's Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, which came at the start of the war between the United States and Iran, as well as the U.S. airstrike that killed Iranian General Qasem Soleimani in 2020. ISRAEL SHARES INTELLIGENCE WARNING IRAN PLOTTED NEW ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT AGAINST TRUMP: REPORT "I don't think it's any secret, it's been in the media, that Iran has publicly said they want to kill President Trump," Deputy Director of the U.S. Secret Service Matt Quinn told reporters at an event last month. The video came amid threats from the Trump administration to nations that fail to sever their economic ties with Tehran and an ongoing naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. In July, Trump secretly switched planes from Air Force One to another aircraft in Turkey via a catering truck due to a credible Iranian surface-to-air missile threat. articles.title: What has happened in Plaid Cymru's first 100 days in power?
articles.summary: Plaid ministers say they are making good progress but the opposition say little has been achieved.
articles.body:
Plaid Cymru claimed victory in celebratory scenes on the steps of the Senedd in May, after it inflicted a heavy and historic defeat on Welsh Labour.

Since then it has been an occasionally rough ride for Rhun ap Iorwerth's minority administration.

After 100 days in charge Plaid ministers say they have laid the foundations to improve public services, and have already made a "tangible" impact in areas like childcare.

But the government failed to get over its first significant hurdle in the Senedd, when its supplementary budget was rejected by the entire Senedd opposition.

Meanwhile opposition parties claim little has changed since Plaid took charge.

Plaid Cymru formed the first non-Labour Welsh government in May, with the party six seats short of a majority of 49.

It won the election on a platform of challenging Westminster to give Wales more control over its own affairs, a promise of a major programme to boost childcare, and to cut waiting times.

The party set out a plan for the first 100 days ahead of the election, which it said showed how serious it was about governing.

It was criticised at the time as a "plan to have a plan", with the party promising to commission a number of reviews or strategies.

The Welsh government said it had made progress on a number of issues in its first few months, including extending free school meals to more secondary school pupils, a new north-south coach service, and a multi-year funding deal for farmers.

But there's a been a focus on a few big areas over the last few months.

Early on Plaid came under pressure to spell out how it would deliver its landmark childcare policy, which would see free care expanded over a four-year period.

Currently parents in work or training can get up to 30 hours a week for children aged three or four. Plaid want to expand this so at least 20 hours is available from nine months to four years old.

Opposition parties have repeatedly pressured Plaid ministers for answers as to how this will work, demanding costings and a timetable for how the expanded scheme will work - leading a minister to promise more detail .

There were questions from councils , who said the proposal faced serious challenges because of a lack of resources and staff.

The Welsh government now says that all local authorities are on track to provide 12.5 hours of free child-care to two-year-olds via the Flying Start scheme by next March.

Plaid ministers want to phase the rest of the scheme over time - but until that is spelled out the party will continue to face scrutiny over how it's achieved.

The length of time that patients have to wait in the NHS was a totemic problem faced by the previous Welsh Labour government.

Plaid Cymru was careful not to raise expectation of an immediate improvement, telling the BBC last February that the public would not expect a difference within the first 100 days .

The party promised to get waiting times "down to pre-pandemic levels" within four years. In June, the Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor said he would eradicate two-year waits in a matter of months .

The latest figures saw two-year waits drop slightly - by 3% to just under 4,100 pathways - but for the third month in a row the total numbers waiting for treatment has risen.

Government Efficiency Minister Dafydd Trystan Davies said the government was laying "the foundations for success to bring down waiting lists" - pointing to work on surgical hubs and a workforce plan.

Plaid is in a minority in the Senedd and the party is vulnerable to defeats if the opposition votes against it.

That happened a few times before the summer recess, including in a crucial vote on an extra £300m in spending to reduce NHS waits and expand childcare.

Labour had demanded £100m extra to be spent on children with additional learning needs - and the two sides had failed to come to an agreement.

It was the first time a Welsh government has lost a vote on a supplementary budget - which is in addition to the main budget exercise that happens in the autumn.

Laura McAllister, professor of politics at Cardiff University, said she thought the government had been a little naive.

"If you're in that position of being a minority government, transactional relationships and goodwill between the parties is absolutely fundamental."

Since then, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has indicated that he does want a budget deal with Plaid .

The Plaid government faced its first major incident over the summer as a devolved government when a number of wildfires broke out in Wales.

The Welsh government came under scrutiny for its crisis management, because unlike the police, fire services are devolved in Wales.

There was criticism from Reform Wales about the time taken in to bring in the army and aerial support .

A minister said lessons needed to be learned with wildfires more likely in the future due to climate change.

Plaid Cymru wants powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure and the Crown Estate to be devolved from Westminster to Cardiff.

It promised negotiations with Westminster to do that, but turmoil in London has made making the case tricky.

Ap Iorwerth tried and failed to get a meeting with the previous prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, although the man now in charge, Andy Burnham, held his first face-to-face meeting with the first minister in July .

Burnham has promised to put devolution front and centre of his government.

But his Welsh Secretary, Stephen Kinnock, has said he is not yet "entirely convinced" by the case for more responsibilities for the Welsh government.

Some at Collier's Adventure Farm in Nelson, Caerphilly, were willing to give the Plaid Cymru government time before rushing to judgement.

Raydean Thomas said: "I think they're finding their feet at the moment. Nothing that they've done has been wrong as far as I can say. I think they're thinking of things in the right way."

Faye Dalgleish-McGee said: "People do rush to have an opinion a bit too quickly - let them get settled in before we start complaining."

Meanwhile, Trish Garner said it was important to wait to see what their plans are.

"But I don't hear an awful lot about what they're going to do and that's my feeling," she added.

Michael Davies said his life had not changed since Plaid had got into power, and that politics was the "same old story" with successive governments blaming each other.

"[They say] it's going to take us x amount of years to put it right and then nothing seems to happen."

Julie Jones, who was also at the coffee morning, said it was too soon to judge ap Iorwerth, but that "he came in all guns blazing".

Dafydd Trystan Davies said that "the initial work has been completed on the 96 actions" in the party's 100-day plan.

He said that in some areas the administration had "put the foundations for success in place".

"But in others, we've made tangible real progress that people will be able to feel already," he said.

The first minister is on leave until the end of the week and was unavailable for interviews ahead of the completion of 100 days in government.

Asked by BBC Wales whether that meant the government was playing down the milestone, Davies said it was him that was responsible for 100-day programme and that ap Iorwerth will issue a "progress report" next week.

Reform accused Plaid of focusing too much on "reviews, committees and plans".

Dan Thomas, Reform's Welsh leader, told BBC Wales that things have "just got worse" since Plaid won the election, with waiting lists having "gone up".

"The first minister said during the election campaign that two-year waits would be eradicated within a matter of months. We're now three months into a Plaid government and we're nowhere near seeing those waits being eradicated."

Ken Skates, leader of Welsh Labour, said there was "quite a contrast" between Plaid Cymru's first 100 days and the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

"We've seen plans and processes here, discussion, a lot of talk, very little action. In contrast with Andy Burnham, we've seen some really, really big interventions that are going to make a difference to people's lives."

Darren Millar MS, Leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd, said: "Plaid's first 100 days have been a disappointing series of missed opportunities to turn the page on 27 years of Labour rule in Wales."

articles.title: Sara Netanyahu verbally abused PMO employee 'daily,' NIS 450,000 lawsuit alleges
articles.summary: Ben-Hamo's lawsuit is not the first filed by a PMO employee over Sara's treatment; another employee received tens of thousands of shekels in compensation aft...
articles.body:
Ben-Hamo's lawsuit is not the first filed by a PMO employee over Sara's treatment; another employee received tens of thousands of shekels in compensation after a settlement, according to KAN News.

Sara Netanyahu verbally abused and made extreme demands of a person employed at the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), N12 News reported on Tuesday, citing a lawsuit filed by the employee against the office.

The lawsuit alleges that the employee, Rami Ben-Hamo, suffered "unacceptable" working conditions, as well as shouting, insults, derogatory nicknames, and humiliation at the hands of Sara "on a daily basis," demanding NIS 450,000 in compensation.

Ben-Hamo claims he fulfilled "every assignment" Sara gave him, resulting in up to 80 overtime hours each month, an amount beyond what his contract allowed for, N12 reported.

He noted that the treatment worsened towards the end of his employment, with Sara allegedly telling him that he is a "bad cleaner" who "doesn't know how to clean."

The employee further alleged that cleaning wipes were thrown on the ground next to him when he missed any dirt spots while cleaning, an issue Ben-Hamo faced due to vision problems.

According to the lawsuit, the PMO did nothing to help Ben-Hamo despite being fully aware of the issues he faced.

Additional insults directed towards Ben-Hamo by Sara allegedly include "You destroyed my family" and "The prime minister and I don't like you," as well as reffering to him as a "primitive Moroccan," according to N12.

The lawsuit further alleges that the poor treatment continued following a heart attack suffered by Ben-Hamo, with the employee deciding to quit after a misunderstanding resulted in Sara throwing a bottle of soda on the floor.

According to N12, Ben-Hamo said aloud that he wanted God to "take me [him] away from this job," with Sara accusing him of having said "May God take her away," and Sara going so far as to inform Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of the incident once he returned home that day.

Additional lawsuits filed against PMO by employees over Sara's behavior

Ben-Hamo's lawsuit is not the first filed by a PMO employee over Sara's treatment, with another employee receiving tens of thousands of shekels in compensation following a settlement , KAN News reported on May 11.

The anonymous employee claimed that Sara humiliated and harassed her, including an alleged incident where Sara threw olives and tomatoes at the employee, causing damage to her clothing.

Miriam Sela-Eitam contributed to this report.

articles.summary: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is urging AI executives to embrace Pope Leo XIV‘s human-centered approach to artificial intelligence after meeting with the pontiff...
articles.body:

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is urging AI executives to embrace Pope Leo XIV 's human-centered approach to artificial intelligence after meeting with the pontiff and discussing his Magnifica Humanitas encyclical.

Khanna Cites Pope Leo's AI Ethics Vision

On Saturday, Khanna said on X that he recently met with Leo to discuss "Magnifica Humanitas" and the ethical challenges surrounding artificial intelligence.

"It was an honor to discuss Magnifica Humanitas with Pope Leo last week," Khanna wrote.

Still Learning the Market? These 50 Must-Know Terms Can Help You Catch Up Fast

He said the pope has offered "an ethical framework for AI affirming human agency & equality."

articles.title: Israel removes Netherlands representatives from Gaza center following settlement goods ban
articles.summary: In a statement released on X/Twitter, Sa’ar highlighted the Netherlands’s recent ban on the import of products made in Israeli West Bank settlements as an ex...
articles.body:
In a statement released on X/Twitter, Sa'ar highlighted the Netherlands's recent ban on the import of products made in Israeli West Bank settlements as an example of Dutch anti-Israel policies.

Representatives of the Netherlands will be expelled from Kiryat Gat's International Support Center for Gaza due to the Dutch government's adoption of anti-Israel legislation, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced on Tuesday.

According to Sa'ar, the expulsion was ordered with the approval of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , and the Dutch Embassy was notified on Tuesday evening.

"Our message is clear: Those who act against Israel will have no foothold in the region. Israel will not allow measures to be taken against it without a response," he asserted.

The representatives will be expelled from the center, previously known as the Civil-Military Coordination Center (CMCC), immediately and must leave the country within one week.

Dutch ban on West Bank goods accompanied by wave of antisemitism

Sa'ar noted that the Dutch government's anti-Israel policies have been accompanied by a wave of antisemitism in the Netherlands .

In a statement released on X/Twitter, Sa'ar highlighted the Netherlands's recent ban on the import, sale, and purchase of products made in Israeli West Bank settlements and the Golan Heights.

The ban was proposed in May of this year, made official in late July, and will take effect on September 22.

When the ban was proposed, a government press release said Dutch nationals and entities inside and outside the Netherlands would be prohibited from buying, selling, or providing intermediary services related to goods produced in settlements.

The Dutch cabinet claimed that the ban was aimed at preventing "Dutch economic activities from contributing to the perpetuation of a situation that is contrary to international law.

Mathilda Heller contributed to this report.

articles.title: Judge Jeanine Hit With Fresh Humiliation Over Trump’s Violent Call
articles.summary: Jeanine Pirro is taking heat from a legal watchdog for her boss’ deranged threat to lawmakers. The Legal Accountability Center has filed a bar complaint agai...
articles.body:
Jeanine Pirro is taking heat from a legal watchdog for her boss' deranged threat to lawmakers.

The Legal Accountability Center has filed a bar complaint against Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, over her participation in President Donald Trump's revenge tour against six Democratic lawmakers who urged the military to reject unlawful commands.

The watchdog urged the New York Attorney Grievance Committee to investigate Pirro, 75, for ordering her subordinates to seek the indictments of six lawmakers—Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly, Reps. Chris Deluzio, Maggie Goodlander, Chrissy Houlahan, and Jason Crow—in connection with a November 2025 video telling the military to defy President Donald Trump's illegal orders.

Pirro "knew or should have known" that her directive to her subordinates "was unwarranted, frivolous, and would serve merely to harass or maliciously injure the targets of her order," the group argued.

"She knew or should have known, as a government prosecutor, that her directive to seek indictments was not legally or factually supported by 'probable cause,'" it added, describing Pirro's conduct as "prejudicial to the administration of justice" and a violation of supervisory obligations.

The complaint stems from a video that six Democrats released last year. They spoke directly to U.S. service members and the intelligence community, reminding them that they took an oath to the U.S. Constitution and that they "can refuse illegal orders."

The video sent Trump into a tailspin, reposting one concerning social media post that read, "HANG THEM GEORGE WASHINGTON WOULD !!"

"This is really bad, and Dangerous to our Country," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Their words cannot be allowed to stand. SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR FROM TRAITORS!!! LOCK THEM UP???"

Pirro quickly fell in line by coming after the six lawmakers, but the effort ultimately fell short when a grand jury refused to indict them.

"Regarding the requirement of 'probable cause,' it should be evident that Ms. Pirro knew or should have known that none existed," the Legal Accountability Center said.

"How could it, when the comments at issue were plainly protected First Amendment speech, when even the Secretary of Defense had said virtually the same thing before he entered the government, and when the principle of not following 'illegal' orders was doctrinally ingrained in all of our military academies? This was purely selective prosecution in its most obvious and improper guise," it added.

Tim Lauer, a spokesperson for Pirro, blasted the complaint as frivolous.

"The grand jury, not the prosecutor, decides whether to indict. That is their job. Attempting to weaponize the disciplinary process against prosecutors for doing their jobs amounts to nothing more than a frivolous complaint," he said in a statement .

The complaint is the latest in a series of embarrassing flubs for Pirro. Earlier this month, she was forced to drop charges against individuals suspected of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after the damages were attributed to "flawed installation by the contractors."

articles.title: Instagram head Mosseri, at children's addiction trial, says few teenagers knew of safety feature
articles.summary: By Greg Bensinger, Diana Novak Jones and Jonathan Stempel OAKLAND, California, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The top executive at Instagram said few teenagers used a ke...
articles.body:
Meta faces a landmark trial in federal court in Oakland

By Greg Bensinger, Diana Novak Jones and Jonathan Stempel

OAKLAND, California, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The top executive at Instagram said few teenagers used a key safety feature to limit their use before it was turned on by default, at a trial over whether Meta Platforms designed Instagram and Facebook to addict children.

Adam Mosseri, the head ‌of Instagram since 2018, denied any suggestion by U.S. states suing Meta that Instagram stalled by not making the "Take a Break" feature the default setting for teenagers until ‌September 2024, nearly three years after its launch.

Under questioning from Jason Slothouber, an attorney for Colorado, Mosseri acknowledged that the percentage of teenagers using Take a Break was in the low-single digits before Instagram made it the default.

Mosseri estimated ​in a December 2021 blog post when Take a Break was launched that in early tests more than 90% of teenage users who turned the feature on kept it on. The feature encourages users to close Instagram after set periods of time.

"Most teens didn't want it," Mosseri said in the fourth day of a trial in Oakland, California, federal court. "We decided to push forward with it anyway."

Mosseri is a central witness in the lawsuit by 29 U.S. states, in what experts call the biggest legal test yet of social media's effects on young users.

Four of the states — ‌California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey — have accused Meta of designing ⁠the platforms to hook young users, fueling anxiety, depression and even suicide, while misleading consumers about their safety.

All 29 states say Meta violated federal law by improperly collecting and using personal data of children under 13 while they used its platforms.

The states have indicated they could seek nearly $200 billion in civil ⁠penalties.

Meta has rejected accusations it sought to addict children, and said its research showed no clear link between adolescents' social media use and a lack of well-being.

INSTAGRAM CHIEF DENIES HIDING SAFETY DATA

Under questioning by Slothouber, Mosseri rejected the idea that he knew of an alleged Meta policy for lawyers to review internal presentations to scrub information from them, or shield him from problems.

Mosseri said it was important that any information Instagram ​had ​about children's safety that became public be high-quality, and backed by experts.

"I am not trying to encourage my team ​to hide anything," Mosseri said. "I want to understand how things work. I ‌can't think of any time that I've encouraged people to bring less information to me."

Mosseri also said Instagram centralized people working on sensitive research about teenagers to a single team and reduced access to the information across the company following the 2021 leak of the so-called Facebook Files.

That leak came from whistleblower Frances Haugen, a former Facebook product manager who said Meta knew its products were unsafe for children but did nothing in order to pursue higher profit.

The trial is expected to resume with more testimony from Mosseri on Wednesday.

DESIGN CHIEF ACKNOWLEDGES SAFETY DATA REMOVAL

Prior to Mosseri's testimony, Instagram director of product design Francesco Fogu testified about a presentation on teenagers' safety that his team prepared in 2023 for Instagram leadership.

Under questioning from Slothouber, Fogu acknowledged the removal of data ‌from a presentation slide showing that teenage Instagram users saw 1.5 times more bullying, suicide, hate, nudity and ​violent content than adult users.

Later, when questioned by a Meta attorney, Fogu said the figure appeared on a different ​slide.

Fogu also said Instagram knew that fewer people would use "Take a Break" by not ​making it the default setting.

Jurors are expected to issue an advisory verdict. U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers will decide ‌whether Meta is liable and, if so, determine any civil penalties and ​changes to Facebook and Instagram.

Mosseri also testified in ​February in a Los Angeles trial that Instagram cared about children's safety, defending its design choices against allegations by company insiders that its features were harmful.

Jurors in that case found Meta and Alphabet's Google negligent in designing their platforms, and ordered them to pay $6 million to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube as ​a child.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $567 ‌million to address teenagers' mental health after that state's attorney general called its platforms a public nuisance.

Tennessee is also suing Meta, raising similar claims about Instagram, in ​a case on trial in Nashville.

(Reporting by Diana Novak Jones in Chicago, Greg Bensinger in Oakland, California and Jonathan Stempel in New York; Additional reporting by ​Nathan Frandino in Oakland and Deborah Sophia in Bengaluru; Editing by Noeleen Walder and Matthew Lewis)

articles.title: Kennedy Center may need to be demolished if not renovated, Justice Department argues
articles.summary: In a Monday court filing, lawyers for the Justice Department argued that the Kennedy Center may need to be torn down if it doesn't receive the renovations pr...
articles.body:
The Justice Department's latest salvo in the battle over the future of the Kennedy Center claims President Trump's "efforts and prestige provide the sole hope for the Center's financial survival, and structural renewal," according to a Monday court filing, which also threatens a possible demolition of the historic building.

Without the president's interventions, says the filing, "the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site."

The filing by the administration's lawyers came in response to the efforts of Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) to block the Kennedy Center board from adding the president's name to the building. The 21-page document argues that the benefits afforded by such an addition make it both necessary and warranted.

"The Board also underscores, and the undisputed evidence demonstrates, that without the prominent recognition of The Trump Administration, and President Trump's efforts, the donors will not contribute, and the Center will continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral," the filing reads. "The Trump Administration, and President Donald J. Trump, should, therefore, be given the respect and dignity of acknowledgement."

The filing also suggests what could replace the center if the building were to be torn down: "a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River … has been proposed, by some, for many years."

"Such a replacement will fail to adequately honor President John F. Kennedy, but would be simpler and more economical to build, operate, and maintain," the administration's lawyers wrote in the filing.

Such a teardown would face enormous legal pushback, but preservation groups are already on high alert after Trump's swift demolition of the White House's East Wing, which was completed before a challenge could be fully mounted.

The Kennedy Center has been mired in controversy since Trump fired its board and had himself appointed chairman in the early months of his second term. Artist and staff defections became common after that, but the question of the center's survival came into stark relief in early February when Trump declared his intention to shutter the center for two years of renovations.

That decision arrived after the Kennedy Center board voted in December to add Trump's name to the building. Both the closure and the renaming were halted in a May ruling by Federal District Court Judge Christopher R. Cooper, who is still overseeing the legal back-and-forth over the center's fate.

Cooper originally gave the administration until mid-June to remove Trump's name from the building. The administration complied but placed a tarp over the sign, which has remained ever since.

This month the board voted to move forward with the renovation, and also to again add Trump's name to the building with the words, "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

The most recent court filing claiming the center's survival rests with Trump conflicts with a recent Washington Post investigation that found the center's revenue plunged after Trump's name was added to the building.

articles.title: Map shows congressional races now toss-ups in districts Trump won
articles.summary: The shifts in the races are notable because both Florida and Michigan backed Trump statewide in 2024.
articles.body:
The 2026 House map is showing new signs of potential vulnerability for Republicans, with races shifting toward Democrats in districts that President Donald Trump carried in the 2024 presidential election.

The latest changes from the nonpartisan Cook Political Report include two races moving from "Lean Republican" to "Toss Up"—Florida's 14th Congressional District and Michigan's open 10th District. Michigan's 8th District, meanwhile, pivoted from "Lean Democrat" to "Likely Democrat."

The shifts are notable because both Florida and Michigan backed Trump statewide in 2024. Trump won Florida with more than 6.1 million votes and carried Michigan with about 2.82 million votes, narrowly defeating former Vice President Kamala Harris in the swing state that had backed ex-President Joe Biden in 2020. The districts themselves also backed Trump in 2024, underscoring the potential significance of Cook's latest ratings. In Michigan, Trump carried the 10th by roughly 7 points and the 8th by about 2 points, Cook highlights.

Newsweek reached out to the White House via email on Tuesday for comment.

The three shifts highlight how the 2026 midterm landscape could put Republican incumbents under pressure even in districts that historically have been favorable to the GOP.

Midterm elections are commonly seen as a measure of public approval for the current president too, and the president's party has traditionally lost seats during these elections. At present, Republicans maintain a narrow House majority, controlling 218 seats, while Democrats hold 212.

With control of the House up for grabs in the upcoming midterm, even modest shifts in Democrats' favor could be consequential.

Florida's 14th District presents a particularly interesting test. The Tampa-area quadrant is represented by Democratic Representative Kathy Castor, but Cook previously rated the contest as Lean Republican following redistricting. The race is now considered a Toss Up after Florida's primary elections established the November matchup and new information, including polling, gave Democrats a stronger position, Cook says. According to Cook's analysis, Trump would have won the newly redrawn district in 2024 by 11 percent.

Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Tuesday, "The shift of Florida's 14th from Lean Republican to toss up is notable but fits the broader pattern of ratings moving toward Democrats as the midterm environment hardens."

Agranoff continued: "Redistricting made the seat more Republican on paper, with Trump carrying the new lines by double digits, so it does not lean Democratic in a structural sense. What it does show is that a well-established incumbent like Kathy Castor can still keep a redrawn district competitive when the national climate is difficult for the party in power. The other two moves in Michigan point in the same direction. This is less about any single Florida race flipping blue and more about how the map is responding to current political conditions."

Michigan's 10th District is also moving into Toss Up territory as an open seat. It includes parts of southeastern Michigan and does not have an incumbent seeking reelection after Representative John James left the House to run for governor. Trump won the district in 2024, making the increasingly competitive race another example of Democrats challenging Republicans in territory that favored the president just two years ago.

The latest changes build on a broader pattern of movement across the 2026 House map, with Democrats aiming to seize on a political environment that has seemingly become more favorable to them as the midterms approach.

Cook's ratings are not predictions of the final outcome, but rather assessments of the expected competitiveness of each race. With primary contests largely settled and general-election matchups taking shape, districts that once appeared relatively safe for Republicans are increasingly becoming battlegrounds—potentially giving Democrats more opportunities to make gains in November.

Meanwhile, Cook has shifted Michigan's 8th Congressional District from "Lean Democrat" to "Likely Democrat" following Republican primary turmoil. Trump-endorsed candidate Amir Hassan unexpectedly lost the August 4 primary to Tom Smith, who had previously dropped out of the race, leaving Smith with less than three months to build a campaign against incumbent Democratic Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet.

McDonald Rivet won the district by 7 points in 2024, even as Trump carried it by 2, Cook notes, and she enters the general election with a significant war chest advantage.

articles.title: Trump threatens to change Lake Ontario's name as trade war with Canada heats up
articles.summary: President Trump said the U.S. is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" amid an escalating trade fight with Canada.
articles.body:
Washington — President Trump threatened Tuesday to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" amid an escalating trade fight with Canada.

"The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America," Mr. Trump said in a post on Truth Social Tuesday morning, claiming the U.S. doesn't expect to be "doing much business with Ontario any longer."

Mr. Trump's comments came as tense trade dynamics with the U.S.' northern neighbor have come to a head in recent days, in the latest dustup between two historically allied countries. On Saturday, the U.S. began imposing 50% tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods after negotiators failed to reach an agreement to resolve the standoff over trade between the key partner countries, prompting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to promise new retaliatory tariffs against the U.S.

On Monday, Mr. Trump announced that the U.S. will impose a 50% tariff on all Canadian automotive and steel imports beginning in January, while claiming that "Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years."

"Canada will be treated like a State no longer!" Mr. Trump added.

Lake Ontario sits between Ontario, Canada's most populous province, and New York state. Mr. Trump and Ontario's Premier Doug Ford sparred on Monday, with Ford calling the U.S. president a "loser" and a "dictator" and pledging to "fight with everything we have."

During his second term, Mr. Trump has repeatedly made threats to make Canada into the 51st U.S. state and sparred with Canadian leaders over trade, NATO, and a dispute over a Detroit-area bridge.

The apparent consideration comes after Mr. Trump announced as he returned to office in early 2025 that he planned to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America," and he later signed an executive order to that effect. The name change was applied to federal references, but other nations are not required to recognize the name.

articles.title: She Listed a Cocktail Lounge and an Apartment as Her Home, Prosecutors Say. Five Felony Charges Later, She Quit the Council Race
articles.summary: A Stockton City Council candidate has formally ended her campaign five days after prosecutors charged her with five felonies over claims that she used addres...
articles.body:
A Stockton City Council candidate has formally ended her campaign five days after prosecutors charged her with five felonies over claims that she used addresses where she did not live to qualify for the race.

Desiree Lynch was running for the District 5 seat when San Joaquin County prosecutors accused her of falsely registering to vote and filing candidate paperwork using Stockton addresses that did not reflect where she actually lived.

Investigators say one address Lynch identified as her residence was associated with Harry's Cocktail Lounge. Another was an apartment at Doyle Garden Apartments. Prosecutors allege she was actually living in Lodi and North Stockton.

Lynch formally withdrew from the race Aug. 24, according to FOX40 . Her exit followed a turbulent stretch in which she announced she was leaving the campaign, reversed that decision four days later and was arrested the following morning.

Prosecutors Say She Used Two Addresses to Establish District 5 Residency

The criminal case centers on whether Lynch actually lived in the council district she was seeking to represent. The San Joaquin County District Attorney's Office says investigators determined that she used two Stockton addresses to establish residency in District 5 while actually residing in Lodi and North Stockton, which is within District 1.

The District Attorney's Aug. 19 announcement identified one location as Harry's Cocktail Lounge at 407 E. Charter Way, also known as East Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard, and the other as Doyle Garden Apartments at 625 E. Oak Street.

There is a small discrepancy in the public records. A criminal complaint later obtained by Stocktonia lists Lynch's first alleged residence as 409 rather than 407 in the same block. The District Attorney's Office had not publicly explained the difference.

Three Filings Became Three Perjury Counts

A criminal complaint obtained by Stocktonia identifies three filings at the center of the perjury allegations. Prosecutors say Lynch signed voter registration paperwork under penalty of perjury on Nov. 10, 2025, using the Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard address.

On Feb. 5, she allegedly filed another voter registration document listing the East Oak Street apartment. The third count concerns nomination and candidacy paperwork Lynch signed March 2 to run for the District 5 seat.

Two additional felony counts accuse her of knowingly registering to vote where she was not entitled to register and filing a false nomination paper or declaration of candidacy.

She Left the Race, Returned and Was Arrested the Next Morning

Lynch first announced Aug. 14 that she would stop campaigning, citing concerns involving her safety, health and family. Four days later, she reversed course and notified the city clerk that she intended to remain in the contest against incumbent Councilmember Brando Villapudua.

The following morning, Aug. 19, Lynch was arrested following a six-week investigation by the District Attorney's Bureau of Investigations. She was booked on five felony counts with bail set at $100,000 and released on bond later that day.

On Aug. 24, Lynch submitted a signed letter withdrawing her candidacy effective immediately. Her attorney, Allen Sawyer, said she would focus on her daughter and family responsibilities while dealing with the criminal case.

Ending Her Campaign Does Not Remove Her From the Ballot

Lynch's decision to stop campaigning does not appear to remove her name from the Nov. 3 general election ballot. When she first announced her withdrawal, Stockton's interim city clerk said her name would remain because she had already advanced from the June primary.

California Elections Code generally prevents a candidate nominated at a primary from withdrawing from the ensuing general election except under limited statutory circumstances.

Lynch's Aug. 24 letter asked the city clerk to remove her name from consideration "as permitted by law," but the latest reporting did not indicate that election officials had authority to grant that request.

Lynch and Villapudua advanced from the June 2 primary after Villapudua received 1,173 votes and Lynch received 1,054, a difference of 119 votes.

She Faces Up to Six Years and Eight Months if Convicted on All Counts

Lynch is scheduled to be arraigned Sept. 2 in San Joaquin County Superior Court. The District Attorney's Office says the five felony counts carry a combined maximum sentence of six years and eight months in state prison if she is convicted on all of them.

Her release conditions include pretrial monitoring, restrictions on leaving California without court approval and a prohibition on possessing firearms or other deadly weapons while the case is pending. The charges remain allegations. Lynch has not been convicted, and prosecutors will have to prove the case in court.

California Has a Formal Process for Reporting Suspected Election Fraud

People who believe they have evidence of false voter registration, candidate filings or another election-related violation do not need to conduct their own investigation.

The California Secretary of State accepts election fraud complaints through its Investigative Services unit. The state's complaint form asks for specific facts such as dates, locations and potential witnesses so authorities can determine whether an Elections Code violation should be investigated.

Suspected violations can also be reported to county election officials or local law enforcement. The San Joaquin County District Attorney specifically asks people with information about election fraud to contact its Bureau of Investigations or Public Integrity Unit.
